Mr. Speaker, if I am in order, I wish to rise to a question of privilege.

On the orders of the

At any time.

rise at any time to a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I
have had an opportunity of perusing in Hansard of yesterday the remarks addressed to the house by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) on the question of privilege then raised by him. I am glad to see him in his seat, and I am sorry that when he had occasion to make those remarks-in which I appear to be slightly interested-unfortunately I had not arrived.
Needless to say, sir, I very cheerfully and very readily accept what my hon. friend then chose to state as being the condition of his own-shall I say?-affairs so far as they relate to the steamship-I should say the schooner W. C. Kennedy. However, it does devolve upon me as a matter of privilege to make some reply to what my hon. friend then asserted. At page 1918 of unrevised Hansard I find that he objects to my designation of "steamship", and I cheerfully make the correction and acknowledge that I should have described the Kennedy as a schooner.
[Mr. Adshead.l
On the same page I find my hon. friend said that I was in error in saying that at the time of the seizure of the Kennedy he was its owner. Again, I cheerfully accept his statement, but until yesterday the only information available to me in regard to the ownership of the schooner was that given under oath before the special committee of this house which in 1926 investigated the Department of Customs and Excise. At the bottom of page 1918 of Hansard my hon. friend is reported as follows:
If I remember correctly, I sold the W. C. Kennedy in 1923, about six months before she was illegally seized-mark you, not legally, but illegally seized-in Northumberland straits nine and a half miles east by south of Pictou island. At the time of this illegal seizure I had no interest whatever in the schooner,-
The remarks that I addressed to the house in connection with this matter on Tuesday last-not by way of any criticism of my hon. friend but on a resolution in amendment of the Customs Act to prevent smuggling- certainly did come from me on the assumption and in the honest belief that my hon. friend was at that time the owner of the boat. My reasons for so concluding are to be found in the statement by Percy D. Rafuse, master of the W. C. Kennedy, which will be found at page 1202 of the proceedings of the special committee which in 1926 investigated the Department of Customs and Excise. Let me quote it for the benefit of the house:
Statement of Percy D. Rafuse, captain boat W. C. Kennedy.
Q. What is your name?-A. Percy D. Rafuse, Lunenburg, Nova Scotia.
Q. Are you a British subject?-A. Yes.
Q. Are you the master of the Kennedy?- A. I am a certified master.
Q. Of what tonnage is the Kennedy?-A. 112 tons.
Q. Where is she registered?-A. Lunenburg, Nova Scotia.
Q. To whom does the Kennedy belong?-A. To Mr. William Duff. Lunenburg, that is as far as I know, but she is under charter to Ronald Betts and Charles Mee.
Q. Who pays you your wages?-A. Mr. Duff, also the crew but I have a telegram from Mr. Duff instructing me to take my orders from Mr. Mee.
Q. By whom are you employed?-A. By Mr. William Duff, Lunenburg, N.S.
Q. How long were you hovering off the place I found you?-A. About three days or three and one-half days.
Your Honour will readily appreciate that, gladly hailing as I do my hon. friend's statement yesterday, I might well be forgiven down to the time of that very convincing explanation for thinking that my hon. friend was the owner of the schooner W. C. Kennedy at the date on which the master so emphatically swore that he was.

Treaty with Spain
I notice also that my hon. friend has taken exception-it is apparent in the paragraph to which I have alluded-to the statement in regard to the boat having been seized for hovering. I have just read what was stated about the hovering that occurred, and I find on page 1194 of the report of the special customs committee the following statement by the chairman, the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier):
I must remark that this is a question of law. Each one of us may interpret this question as we like, but I would like, if there is an opinion given by the Department of Justice, to see it.
Mr. R. L. Calder, K.C., counsel for the committee who had gone over the file, answered :
The entire file reveals no opinion, but the action was taken by the Customs department, merely on the representations of the owners of the vessel, that that was the true legal position. Without referring to the Department of Justice, the decision was made.
May I say again that, with the very best intention in the world to do justice to my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough, no one can legitimately complain that I accepted these statements without reserve from the sworn evidence given before the customs committee. I was not present yesterday, but my hon. friend felt called upon to make some comments on certain things that had occurred when I visited Lunenburg in the campaign of 1926. I shall not attempt to follow him there, but I would say-Sufficient unto the election is the campaign speech thereof. I am willing to leave the matter at that.
Mr. Speaker, I presume-
Order.
There can be no debate on the explanation given by the hon. member.

I am rising to a question of privilege and I think I am within the rules of the house in replying to the statements made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell, Hamilton), in his attempt at an extenuation of the remarks he made in this house the day before yesterday. You will have noticed that the hon. member did not refer to what he had said about my being president of the company owning the cargo of the W. C. Kennedy, valued at $20,000. He made that statement deliberately and now he offers no excuse and gives no reason for it.

The captain said
you paid him.

thing. I did not pay for or own the whisky. I am talking about the cargo, and the hon. member cannot deny the fact that he stated that I was president of a company which owned the cargo of the W. C. 1.	Is the government considering refusing
to continue the license of the broadcasting station	C.H.C.Y.	Edmonton	(International
Bible Students) ?
2.	If so, for what reason?

In view of the developments in recent times of radio broadcasting and having regard to the seemingly unsatisfactory conditions now obtaining, the government is giving	consideration to	the	question ofwhether or not it would be generally advantageous to adopt a policy of national broadcasting along the lines adopted in this respect	by the	British	government. TheDepartment of	Marine	and	Fisheries is
responsible for the administration of the Radiotelegraph Act under which every radio station in Canada must be licensed. With the advent of broadcasting, the department as the licensing authority, at once realized its responsibilities to the listening public. Each application for a broadcasting license was, with these responsibilities in mind, dealt with as far as practicable from the viewpoint of the broadcast listeners.
When the Bible Students applied for a license to erect and operate a station at Toronto in 1922, their application received very serious consideration, but from information available the department was of opinion that it would not be in the best interests of the public to grant a license and the same was consequently withheld. An application was finally made in 1924 by an individual unit of
the association at Saskatoon for a station at that place. The request for hours of broadcasting appeared modest and upon the recommendation of the department's local inspector that they be given a trial, more particularly for the benefit of the country people in that large farming section of the country, a license was issued to them. Subsequently applications were made and licenses issued to individual units of the association at Vancouver, Edmonton and Toronto, respectively. It may be stated here that all licenses automatically expire at the end of each fiscal year, namely the 31st March. Thus the department is in a position to review the same before granting renewals.
When the licenses for the Bible Students expired at the end of the fiscal year, 1927, some consideration was given to the question whether they should be renewed, because of complaints made by the listening public against the matter broadcast by these stations. It was decided, however, to give the association a further trial and the licenses were extended for another year. While the licenses were originally applied for by individual units of the association at the places named the broadcasting stations appear to have become organized under the central authority at Toronto, who last year made application and in whose name the four licenses were renewed. Whether this reorganization has any connection with the matter is not certain, but complaints from the listening public have gradually increased until to-day the department has received a large number of protests and petitions asking that the broadcasting activities of this association be either curtailed or entirely suspended. The matter being broadcast is generally described by complainants as having became intolerable and that the propaganda carried on under the name of Bible talks is said to be unpatriotic and abusive of all our churches. Evidence would appear to show that the tone of the preaching seems to be that all organized churches are corrupt and in alliance with unrighteous forces that the entire system of society is wrong and' that all governments are to be condemned.
The department'has before it many letters and a petition asking that the Toronto station be closed. A petition from the board of trade at Saskatoon asks that the association's broadcasting from the station at that place be restricted and the local inspector, who originally recommended the granting of the license, says that he has a "continual deluge of complaints." Complaints have been received from officials of the city and provincial authorities against the Edmonton station, and there are many protests from other prominent people in regard to the same station. Finally,
Questions

a joint petition has been received from the Greater Vancouver Radio Aassociation and the Radio Trades Association of Vancouver asking that the license for the Vancouver station located at Burnaby, British Columbia, be not renewed for next year.
It should be emphasized that these communications and petitions are unsolicited, and should be taken as fully representative of the broadcast listeners in general. On the other hand the supporters of the association are protesting against any restriction of their broadcasting activities or the closing of the stations, but we are informed that these protests have been solicited. It should be borne in mind also that in granting licenses after first refusing them the department indicated its entire impartiality in the matter and its willingness to give the association a fair trial, to be either accepted or rejected by the listening public.
There are many who say that if the listener does not want to hear what any particular station has to say he has merely to tune it out. This may be so in some cases, but a large percentage of receivers in use at the present day are not sufficiently selective to do this; especially where the station is in close proximity we know very well that the listener has either to accept the program of the local station or listen to none at all. If we were in the fortunate position of having an unlimited number of radio channels available, it could be well arranged so to place stations broadcasting matter of the character objected to where their transmissions could be easily eliminated, but we have a very limited number of these channels and cannot accommodate all requests. The demand for channels from proposed stations ready to broadcast desirable programs of a high order far exceed the number of channels available, and up to the present we have refused nearly a hundred applications for broadcasting licenses. The i present trend of the listening public is for stations employing high power and providing "entertainment" of the better standard rather than propaganda.
The evidence now before" us would indicate that the broadcasting of the association does not meet with the approval of the listening public, and in reviewing license renewals for the current fiscal year, mindful of its responsibilities to the broadcast listeners as the licensing authority, the department is persuaded that in the general public interest the licenses of the Bible Students' stations should not be renewed.
I may add one further word. In view of the recent development in radio broadcasting,

and having regard to the seemingly unsatisfactory conditions now obtaining, the government are giving consideration to the question whether or not it would be generally advantageous to adopt a policy of national broadcasting along the lines adopted in this respect by the British government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the Geneva Opium convention and protocol signed at Geneva on the nineteenth of February, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five, after the second opium conference, and which was signed, on behalf of Canada by the Canadian representative duly authorized to that effect;
And that this house do approve of same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there have been three important international opium conferences; one at Shanghai in 1909, another at the Hague in 1912, and a conference at Geneva in 1925. At the Hague conference an important convention was agreed to by the nations there represented, and Canada became a party to that convention on December 17, 1912. At the conference at Geneva, Canada was represented by the Hon. Dr. Beland, who at that time was Minister of Health, and by Dr. Amyot, the deputy minister of the department. They were present during most of the sessions, though, owing to the necessity of Dr. Beland having to return to Canada to attend the sittings of this house, his place was taken by Dr. W. A. Riddell, Canadian advisory officer at Geneva. It was decided at Geneva to make more effective the Hague conference of 1912. The terms of the convention and of the protocol are set forth in the document I tabled in the house before the recess. The convention contains thirty-nine articles. They are intended to complete the provisions of the Hague convention of 1912 and to bring about a more effective restriction k>f the production of narcotics in the effort to secure a closer control of the trade, and for the appointment of a permanent central board to watch the international trade. The board will prepare every year a report which will be sent to the contracting parties, and will also make recommendations.
In the protocol the signatory states recognize their obligation under chapter 1 of the Hague convention to establish such a control over opium as will prevent illicit traffic; and they agree to take steps within five years to prevent the smuggling of opium, so as to prevent its unlawful use in the countries where its use is at present authorized.
At the convention at Geneva Dr. Beland was chairman of the most important committee, and, as will be recalled, rendered a highly important international service by bringing about accord between the different countries, as embodied in the agreement subsequently drafted.
The purpose of this motion is to obtain approval by parliament of the convention. It
Geneva Opium Convention

was signed by the Hon. Senator Dandurand, When representing Canada at a subsequent meeting of the League of Nations, and it will be ratified by the king when parliament has given its approval. Canada will then become one of the several countries bound by the terms of this convention. It is desirable that the convention should be approved at once because it binds all countries only after a certain number of the signatories have had the convention approved and ratified.
I think under clause 36 it requires ten of the states to be signatories. How many have signed at present?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will find the signatures at the end of the document which I tabled. There are considerably over ten.

May I ask the Prime Minister why a resolution like this should take from the 19th February, 1925, to the 12th April, 1928, to be brought forward? Are we to be merely a rubber stamp? It appears so. It appears that this was signed on behalf of Canada by the Canadian representative duly authorized in that behalf. If he was authorized, who authorized him? This parliament never authorized him. It seems to me to be a lot of red tape. We are supposed to be a nation. Is parliament to be just a rubber stamp for all the countries bordering the seven seas? It seems to me we are just going around in a circle. Here is a resolution for a convention, and it appears that three years ago it was signed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the International Sanitary convention and of the protocol of signature signed at Paris on the twenty-first of June, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-six, and which was signed, on behalf of Canada, by the Canadian representative acting under full powers issued by His Majesty;
And that this house do approve of same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, from May 10th to June 21st, 1926, an international sanitary conference was held in Paris. The purpose of the conference was to consider effective means, as between the nations, for preventing the spread of communicable diseases. At this convention Canada was represented by Dr. Amybt, the Deputy Minister of the Department of Health. A convention, which I presented to parliament before the Easter recess, was drawn up art; that conference. This convention contains general provisions to be observed by the signatories on the appearance of plague, cholera, yellow fever, and certain other communicable diseases in their territories, and provides for measures of defence against these diseases. Its chief object is to provide with the least interference possible to shipping and transportation, effective procedure based on scientific knowledge for the prevention of the entrance and dissemination of the great epidemic diseases and 6uch others as might become widely epidemic.
On the recommendation of the government of Canada Dr. Amyot received full power from His Majesty the King to sign the convention, and the convention is now being submitted to parliament for its approval.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime
Minister on what theory parliament is called upon to approve this convention. I understand that in Great Britain, when a convention of this nature is executed by His Majesty, it becomes a part of the public law of that country and if it is a convention referring to other parts of the dominions, the empire as a whole, it becomes a part of the public law of those dominions. Does the Prime Minister assume that the approval of this convention by the parliament of Canada makes it a part of the public law of Canada, or is it his intention to provide by statute for carrying into effect within Canada the provisions of the convention with regard to sanitation? I had the opportunity during a part of an evening to read over the provisions of this convention, but it seemed to me to call for

Sanitary Convention-Mr. Mackenzie King
a very large expenditure of public funds, for a large increase in the whole machinery of health inspection at the ports of Canada, and for the provision of new hospitals for dealing with those who, having an infectious disease or having been liable to infection, enter certain Canadian ports. I should like to know briefly:	Does the approval of this convention by the parliament of Canada make the convention the public law of this country? Second, is it the intention to bring into the house legislation by statute to carry the provisions of the convention into full effect? Third, wilt such statutory provisions be enacted to increase the work, I suppose, of the Department of Health and health authorities in the various cities, to extend the hospital system and all the resit, involving a large expenditure of money? Are we to took for such ancillary legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend first with respect to the course of procedure that is being adopted of having parliament approve this convention, that that course is in accordance with the principle underlying a resolution of this house which, was introduced by myself a year or two ago and at the time unanimously adopted. The resolution provided, so far as Canada is concerned, that important treaties should be approved in the first instance by this parliament. That is the reason why this convention, which to all intents and purposes is in the nature of a treaty between different countries, is being submitted to parliament. The purpose is to secure in the last analysis the control of parliament over any agreements of international significance which may bind the people of this dominion. If I caught my hon. friend's remarks aright he asked at the outset, why it should be necessary to have this parliament approve, seeing that His Majesty the King had signed the convention and that that would serve to bind all.

Pardon me. That was not
the point. I was asking as to the effect of this approval. Does this convention become a part of the public law of Canada on the approval of parliament being given?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me present to my hon. friend the development that has taken place in the signing of international agreements of this character. At the time of the Peace conference at Geneva the signature of the British Empire as a whole was given by one of the British ministers. In fact, if my hon. friend looks at the signatures to the Geneva Opium conference, he will see what may on the face of it appear to be something of an anomaly. That agreement
is signed for "the British Empire by Malcolm Delevingne. Then there appears the signature for Canada of Hon. R. Dandurand, and following that the signatures for _ Australia, New Zealand and India of their respective representatives. I understand that at the time of the Peace conference the various governments of the empire represented there found it impossible to arrive at a final agreement as to how the several dominions should have reserved to themselves the right of signature through their own representatives, where they were to be held to be bound by treaties and the signature of the British government held to be for Great Britain alone as contrasted with the British Empire as a whole. My recollection is that there was reached at that time,
I will not call it a compromise but a method of meeting the then existing situation. It was this: while the British representative signed as for "the British Empire", his signature was held to bind only Great Britain and Northern Ireland and in order that the other parts of the empire should be held to be bound the signatures of their respective representatives were to be separately affixed. At the Imperial conference of 1926 that method of procedure was changed and it was then agreed that the practice should be discontinued of having international agreements signed by Great Britain and Northern Ireland under the designation "the British Empire;" that as regards treaties binding different parts of the empire the signature of the representative of Great Britain and Northern Ireland would be as for that part only of the empire which did not include the self-governing dominions and the signatures for the self-governing parts of the empire would be in the names of their respective representatives. In order that this agreement or any other of like significance may bind Canada, it is necessary under our practice to bring to this parliament for approval the convention itself, and that is why the convention is now being submitted. After parliament has given its approval and before the convention becomes binding, His Majesty will be obliged to ratify it. Ratification, as my hon. friend knows, is an act of the crown, of the sovereign, but it is an act so far as Canada is concerned, that will be performed on the advice of the government, given after the approval of parliament has been obtained. Upon ratification the terms of this agreement will bind the Dominion.
My hon. friend has drawn attention to possible expenses. He has pointed out that our approval may necessitate the introducing of many measures that are far-reaching and

The delegate of Canada reserves for his government the right to decide whether, from the point of view of measures to be applied, a foreign area should be considered as infected and to determine the measures which should be applied in special circumstances to arrivals in Canadian ports. Article 12 of the convention is as follows:
_ The government of a country in which an infected area is situated shall inform other governments and the office International d'Hygiene Publique in the manner specified in Article 4, when the danger of infection from that area has ceased, and when all the preventive measures have been taken. On the receipt of this information the measures prescribed in chapter IT. shall no longer be applicable to arrivals from the area in question, except in exceptional circumstances which will require to be justified.
So that, as far as Canada is concerned, this country has been put in the position of determining for itself what enactments may in certain cases be necessary to meet an international menace arising from disease. And so far as statutory enactments may be concerned, it will be for parliament to decide as the occasion arises.

The reservation that it will be within the discretion of the government and parliament of Canada to decide as to the extent to which they will carry it out is more a reservation pro forma than an effective reservation. sponsibilities indeed. But the fact is that a reservation such as that does not diminish the moral responsibility of this country to carry out such conventions to the full extent necessary in order to give full and complete effect to them.
As to the form in which the treaties are now negotiated, I presume that at some other time we may have an opportunity of discussing that matter, but, as I understand it, there is a grave difference of opinion between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and some of us on this side of the house who have given some attention to the subject. In the form which has now been adopted by virtue of the resolutions passed at the conference of 1923, as amended by the Imperial conference of 1926, I understand that Great Britain signs for Great Britain and Ireland, but she signs for more than Great Britain and Ireland; she signs for every part of the British Empire outside of the dominions. Therefore, Great Britain is really signing for the British Empire except for South Africa, Australia, Canada New Zealand, and the Irish Free State.

If I remember correctly-I am speaking solely from memory again, because I have not my notes here-when the Irish Free State sought to appoint a minister plenipotentiary to AVashington, there was a conference held between the Free State government and Mr. Thomas, who was then Secretary of State for the colonies, and they agreed as to the terms of the communication which would be made to the Secretary of State of the United States with regard to the terms and conditions and restrictions under which the Irish Free State would appoint a minister.
Was that not before 1926?

Yes, in 1924, if I remember correctly. In that communication, which has been published in a white paper, which I have read, and which has also been published by the United States in its diplomatic correspondence, the British ambassador at Washington stated to the United States government that the condition upon which an Irish Free State minister would be appointed was that he should deal in his negotiations with the United States government solely and exclusively in relation to those matters which solely and exclusively affected the Irish Free State, and that was the condition on which the United States government agreed to accept the minister. That communication from the British ambassador at Washington to the Secretary of State of the United States-I am sorry I have not it here-went on to state that all matters which affected Great Britain and other parts of the empire, and not the Irish Free State solely and exclusively, would still continue to be dealt with by the British ambassador at Washington. Subsequently I made a motion in this house, to which the Prime Minister agreed, asking that there be brought down the documents in relation to the appointment of the Hon. Mr. Massey as Canadian minister at Washington, and again I am dealing with those documents from memory. Those documents indicated that the Canadian minister was to represent Canada in respect of Canadian affairs. I remember a short time afterwards reading the debates of the British House of Commons-and I shall be glad to give hon. gentlemen the reference- where Mr. Amery was asked, what is the
position of the Canadian minister at Washington? In answer, he referred to the reply that had been given some two or three years before by Mr. Thomas, then Secretary of State for the Colonies, in relation to the appointment of the Irish Free State minister at Washington, and said that the same conditions and restrictions would apply to the work of the Canadian Minister to the United States.
Therefore I assume-and I am simply trying to follow this out in my own mind-that the Imperial conference resolutions effected a constitutional reform. Those resolutions have never been approved by this parliament nor by the Australian parliament nor by the Imperial parliament. I do not know whether they have been approved by the parliament of the Irish Free State, but I see they were approved the other day by the parliament of South Africa. But assuming that they do effect a constitutional reform, I understand it to be this; that Canada, through its representative at Paris or at Washington; may negotiate treaties which solely and exclusively apply to Canada and affect no other part cf the British Empire; that the duties of a Canadian minister at Paris or at Washington are confined and restricted solely to matters which affect Canada, and Canada only, and that he has no jurisdiction to deal with matters which affect Canada in common with her sister dominions and Great Britain or other parts of the empire.
Consequently, in the negotiation of treaties I still understand that if they do not involve active obligations, as this treaty seems to, but only passive obligations-and the Prime Minister must admit, if he looks into it carefully, that there are a hundred and one matters affecting the most precious rights of Canadian citizens in all parts of the British dominions which are only passive obligations -with regard to those passive obligations, this government has acknowledged no duty to submit such treaties for the approval of the Canadian parliament.

speechtext:
This is merely a resolution asking the house to ratify a convention which the representatives of this country have signed on behalf of Canada as a member of the League of Nations. Canada is a member of the League of Nations of its own right. This convention was signed prior to the Imperial conference of 1926, and anything which was done in 1926 has no bearing on the present question. Canada signs a treaty of peace as a member of the League of Nations on an exactly equal status with Great Britain and with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations. Some Canadians do not like it, but even most of those who do not have come to the point where, when speaking publicly, they express pride in our equality in that respect, and claim credit for what is done. And I am pleased that they should claim credit in some way, because after all it shows the trend of public opinion in Canada. This convention has been signed by Canada as a separate member of the League of Nations. It has been signed by "the British Empire," which means Great Britain and Northern Ireland and other parts of the British Empire which are not separate members of the League of Nations. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, there was an anomaly in that respect, and at the Imperial conference of 1926 it was decided unanimously- and the British government agreed-that in future even conventions that are made in the League of Nations will be revised in respect of the title: the words "British Empire" will be replaced by "Great Britain and Northern Ireland" and other parts which are not separate members of the league.
My hon. friend says that the changes which were made at the Imperial conference of 1926 have not been submitted to the British parliament and to the other parliaments. He is right in that regard. But the British government has given effect to those resolutions of the Imperial conference and the League of Nations has been notified that now the title to be given to that part of the empire com-

prising Great Britain and Northern Ireland shall be so designated and shall not be called "the British Empire," which certainly made for confusion. The new conventions and agreements which have been signed since 1926 have carried into effect the provisions of the report of the Imperial conference of that year in that respect.
As to ratification, my hon. friend asked, why should this be submitted to parliament? As the hon. gentleman knows, ratification of treaties and agreements is a formal matter which differs in various countries. In Great Britain ratification is made by His Majesty the King, naturally on the recommendation of his advisers; in other countries it is different. In the United States the senate is the body that ratifies international treaties. I remember that when Mr. Lloyd George submitted to the British parliament the treaty of Peace, he took care to say that under the British constitution it was not really necessary, before His Majesty gave his assent to the ratification of the treaty, that it should be submitted to parliament. He thought it was such an important matter, however, that parliament should approve of it before His Majesty ratified the treaty, and this viewpoint was also accepted by the Canadian government at that time. Mr. Lloyd George said that this did not mean all treaties should be submitted to parliament, while on the other hand there is a strong body of public opinion in Great Britain which believes that all international agreements and treaties should be submitted to and approved by parliament before being ratified by His Majesty. This is the policy of the Labour party, and I believe they are right. This was the view accepted in Canada; a resolution has been passed by this parliament pledging that all treaties shall be submitted to parliament before they are ratified. This Question was discussed casually during the present session, and I may say if there is any treaty coming into effect as the result of negotiations with the United States with regard to water transportation, this house will approve of the treaty or will reject it before it is carried into effect in any way.
My hon. friend spoke about Locarno, and said that the Prime Minister and myself were very good boys when we were over there. He also said that we approved of the treaty of Locarno and that we were morally bound by it. We were not parties to the Treaty of Locarno; we were not represented when it was signed. Included in that treaty was a clause which stated that Canada and the other dominions would be bound if they agreed

to the treaty, but when it was submitted to the Canadian government we took the attitude that ive did not want to be bound by it. As I remember it, we were asked not to take any formal or definite step before the Imperial conference was called, which was to be held at a certain time in 1926. At that Imperial conference the treaty of Locarno was discussed and the dominions were asked to accept it. I hope I am not betraying any confidence now, but I am forced to tell this because of what my hon. friend has said; Canada, took the stand that we would not be bound by that treaty, and in view of the stand taken by Canada and perhaps one or two other dominions, no resolution was brought forward for the purpose of binding the dominions by that treaty. There was a nice little resolution congratulating Sir Austen Chamberlain upon the part he took in bringing about European peace, and I am free to say that he played a fine part at Locarno; as far as I was concerned, I had no objection to congratulating him on the really great work he did there. As far as my country is concerned, however, we never agreed to accept that treaty, and as a Canadian citizen I do not see that Canada should assume obligations in connection with the boundaries between France and Germany, any more than England should assume obligations in connection with the boundaries between Germany and the rest of central Europe. They agreed to guarantee the present boundaries between Germany and Belgium and Germany and France, but they did not agree to guarantee the boundaries between Germany and Poland or the other states of central Europe. One reason was because the eastern boundary was too far from England; well, the western boundary is still further from Canada. I do not believe it would have been good policy for us to assume any obligation which might result in a war to guarantee any boundaries in central Europe or elsewhere outside our own country. I have no objection to stating publicly and openly what my stand was in that regard, and I am willing to submit it to the Canadian people for approval or disapproval.
Might I ask a question? Did not Germany herself guarantee those boundaries?

It was a treaty to
guarantee the present boundaries between Germany and her neighbours; it was for the purpose of keeping peace. I will admit that, and I think it was a good treaty as far as European peace is concerned. However, I do not see why Canada should bind herself by any such treaty. I am free to admit that as a member of the League of Nations Canada has certain obligations, and if she is ever called upon to fulfil them, if there is a war with regard to any of these boundaries, Canada will have to consider what are her obligations as a member of the league. We are a member of the British commonwealth of nations, and we are quite willing to assume all our obligations and responsibilities in that respect. If there is a war, it will be for the Canadian parliament to decide whether the situation of Canada as a member of the British commonwealth of nations would compel this country to take part in that war. This, however, is quite different from binding ourselves to take part in wars with which we have no concern, just because these treaties or agreements might be conducive to the peace of Europe. As I have already said, I think the Locarno treaty was a fine instrument, but I also believe Canada could not be bound by it and should not accept it.
In concluding his remarks the last speaker said he wanted to keep our allegiance to His Majesty the King, and I agree with him absolutely in what he said. I yield to no one in my devotion to the king and in my desire to adhere to that allegiance to His Majesty, but my hon. friend and I differ as to the best way to retain that allegiance. I believe that the present constitution of the British commonwealth of nations is more secure and will be better safeguarded by acknowledging that all the citizens of the different parts of the British commonwealth of nations are equal in status and free to look after their own affairs. We all consider the king as the great bond of unity between us, and we want to keep that bond as sacred as possible.

Mr. Speaker, there are a large number of people and a large section of Canada who do not agree with the ways and means taken outside the British Empire under our new status in signing these conventions. It is all very well for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to stand up in this house in 1928 and ask this honourable body to agree to the sanitaiy conventions on terms adopted in 1926 by delegates who were supposed to represent this parliament, and who had no authority to sign a convention and in my opinion were never authorized to do so. You will notice the wording of the resolution, " and which was signed, on behalf of Canada,

by the Canadian representative acting under full power issued by His Majesty". The first point is as to the status of the representative to sign that convention.
We have in Canada to-day a new disease, the new status disease, which must be cured first and exterminated from the shores of Canada. The Governor General is to-day represented here for the first time in a convention. The Governor General does not represent Downing Street. He is now a mere viceroy. If he were to ask for advice, they would tell him that he possesses in the front benches all the advice which can be given him. He is the representative alone of the government of Canada and cut off from His Majesty entirely. We have been content as a nation to depend upon the mother country, upon the British board of health, the British board of trade, the British Medical Association, and the medical health officers of the country and their organizations and especially on education in these matters. There are two or three hon. members who have spoken in this debate, and who, if they want laws for public health, should start at home. May I say to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that they need a proper Public Health department to look after their public health in the city of Montreal; their water supply should be owned by the city, and that would do more for national public health in Montreal than all the conventions signed at Geneva, Rome, Paris and all the other places on world sanitary matters. Three-fourths of this convention does not apply to Canada at all. What have we to do with disease on the Red sea?
Who are the deputations which have been over the country asking for this legislation? Two or three of these gentlemen come from the city I represent, and they can hardly get together a corporal's guard at their league meetings. It is all very well for Canada's delegates to the League of Nations to waste the country's money on trips to Geneva; and what do I find? I find that instead of these Canadian representatives patronizing Canadian steamship ports they go down to New York. And what do they do when they get over there? Some of them are so-called labour men, and some of them are defeated Liberal candidates from the Toronto district. I know one of them who went over to represent us who knew nothing about public or international health laws. In all the great fights which we have had by Doctor Hastings, I have never known that gentleman to be on the public platform. We have in Toronto a great public health department and a great health officer. Dr. Hastings, one of

If you look over this report in regard to cholera and other diseases you will find they want to regulate the Dead sea, the Suez canal and the seven seas. Whither are we drifting under this new status? If we go on this way I do not know where this parliament is going to land. This convention will not increase the crops of our farmers, but will empty their pockets in payment of taxes which this fad now puts into the form of conventions binding Canada the world over. If the government want to do anything in the way of preventing diseases of this kind and for sanitation, let them start at home and deal with
the diseases from which Canada is suffering to-day. Let them start right in this city of Ottawa and make the city clean up its streets and thus prevent diseases from arising. They do not know how to keep their streets clean; they have the worst kept streets of any city in Canada, and any health officer will tell you that there are more germs and diseases to be found in the streets of a great city than anywhere else. Let us begin at home and let us stop signing all these conventions. If this is a result of our new status, dear knows where we are going to land. If we are going to enforce these conventions we shall have to maintain a large army and navy. Why do we not begin at home by placing on the great lakes life-saving stations for some of our magnificent crews that are handling the great western crop in November and December? Let us not forget that we are part and parcel of the British Empire. Let the government co-operate with the provincial governments and the municipalities in matters of public sanitation and health instead of going off to the Dead sea, the Suez canal and all the countries that border on the seven seas. This sanitary convention is the most remarkable document that I have ever seen in my life and I do not think we should be called upon now to approve a convention set out in a document consisting of forty pages and which was formulated in 1926. The Liberal party held a great sanitary convention in the city of Ottawa and there were twelve pages of recommendations in their platform but not one of them was carried out. I have discussed this proposition with some of the ablest health officers in the country and they do not approve of what is being done. One of the most prominent health officers on this continent told me that it would be far better if Canada would continue in an educational way to work with the British board of trade, the British board of health, our sister dominions and the British Medical Association in matters of public health and sanitation. I protest against this reckless waste of public money in sending all these large deputations over to this mythical League of Nations which is causing more trouble to the British Empire than any other agency I know of to-day. We are part and parcel of the British Empire, and it was a very sorrowful day for this country when we changed the status which had been good enough for Canada for nearly one hundred years, when we departed from that principle and started signing treaties as a separate country regarding Egypt, Persia, Russia and everything the League of Nations proposes to get up. Where will it all end? It is a nice way of spending money for some gentlemen to take a trip to the League of Nations, going via New York instead of patronizing our own ports. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has criticized this convention somewhat and I agree with him that charity begins at home. If the members of this house will see that their own constituencies are properly regulated in regard to health matters, that will be much better for Canada than all these proposals in the convention. We can well leave these sanitary laws so far as the overseas part is concerned, to the British government, the British board of trade, the British Medical Association and the shipping companies who are beyond the control of this parliament.
Mr. J. 8. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):	Mr. Speaker, I should like to have
had a word before the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) spoke, because what I have to say is rather in nature of a question. I quite agree that the procedure adopted by the government in this case is the correct one. It seems to me that parliament ought to ratify these conventions. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that the decisions and resolutions of the Imperial conference ought to have been brought and ought still to be brought before parliament. I think that was done this last year in South Africa in the case of some of the more important decisions reached at the Imperial conference.
In connection with this sanitary convention, I have wondered whether the labour conventions of the league were ever ratified by parliament. I cannot recall that this was the case and I should like to ask the Prime Minister:	If not, why not? Why should we
not ratify the labour conventions which I think are equally binding and perhaps of much

more far-reaching importance than this sanitary convention? So far as I remember, parliament has not had an opportunity of making a declaration on the matter. Someone suggested to me that at that time we had not the status which we have now. I cannot see that that has anything to do with the matter because at that time we were signatory to the peace treaty and we were a member of the League of Nations. I will ask the government why we have not had the ratification by parliament of these other conventions?
Further than that, I am interested as to whether this is to be simply a sort of pious resolution, or whether what has been already suggested is really the case, that this resolution if passed will carry the implication that we are going to proceed to implement this convention. Is that clearly understood? Is it understood that if we pass this resolution to-day it means that the terms of this convention will be implemented by Canada? During the past seven years in which I have been a member of this house I have been trying from time to time to bring up the various clauses of the conventions and treaties which have been passed by the League of Nations, and almost invariably we are told, with regard to each matter, that this is not a matter over which the Dominion government has any jurisdiction whatever. We were so informed in regard to old age pensions; we were so informed in regard to unemployment; we were so informed in regard to the hours' and conditions of labour. All these matters, we were told, under the British North America Act come under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. We have had before the house this session the question of sickness insurance, and there are those who suggest that this is a matter entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. So I would ask with regard to this sanitary convention, are we quite clear that the Dominion of Canada has jurisdiction; I am speaking now of the nation of Canada, not as a part of the British Empire, but in its relation to the several provinces which comprise this Dominion. In this country we seem to have a sort of divided sovereignty. My own contention all along has been that if Canada has the right to make treaties at all, Canada has the right to see that they are enforced; I cannot see that we are a nation otherwise.
In regard to this resolution then, irrespective of the contention that may be put forward by provincial authorities that some of these matters are entirely within the purview of the provinces, in spite of what has been said as to the provinces having control in the matter of certain civil rights and all

Sanitary Convention-Mr. McGibbon
the Test of it, if we endorse this convention, we should undertake to see that it is fully enforced, and that in the event of an outbreak of disease in any one province we shall have the machinery at hand to cope with it and take whatever steps may be necessary. I should like to have the assurance of the government that we are on safe ground, and that this is not merely the "rubber stamping," as someone has put it, of something that has been done by the League of Nations, but rather that we are solemnly entering upon the endorsation of this convention with the understanding that we are to implement it by definite legislation, and that never again will anyone here assert that this is beyond our powers.

In the publication of this report I think the League of Nations has left itself open to a great deal of criticism. It is not that the articles in the so-called convention are not proper, but the fact is they are not agreed to; The protocol, in fact, is nothing but a summary of one nation after the other making reservations in regard to different articles of this convention. If you will look at the protocol you will see that Germany makes a reservation in regard to " observation ", and that Brazil, Chili, the United States of America, and in fact nearly every country signs the articles of this convention with reservations. If we are going to have a convention to which no one is agreeing 100 per cent, what is the use of it? Read the articles one after the other, and you will see that the most important articles in this convention are accepted only with reservations by the different countries.
I wonder if the Prime Minister or the Minister of Health actually realizes what he is agreeing to in this convention. Article 14, for instance, reads:
Governments undertake to maintain in their large ports and in their surroundings, and as far as possible in the other ports and their surroundings, sanitary services possessing an organization and equipment capable of carrying out the application of the prophylactic measures in regard to the diseases mentioned in this convention and especially the measures laid down in articles 6, 8 and 13.
If the Minister of Health were in the house,
I would ask him what preparations he has made in this regard. What lies at the basis of all these articles is the compulsory notification of diseases, and there is not a country in which these diseases arise that has compulsory notification, and each country, one after the other, has signed this convention with reservations simply because they are not able to carry it out. We agree to prepare all our ports to deal with these diseases. Delousing, for instance; what preparations have we at our ports for carrying this out? I think we ought to be assured by the government whether or not they have made preparations to carry out the different articles of this convention-the different methods of preventing mosquitos from getting on boats, delousing, and all this kind of thing. It is worth while reading the different articles of this convention, because then you must come to the conclusion that somebody is making a monkey of us.

It is quite evident to my mind that this legislation is like a lot of other legislation that the government introduce; they hardly know where it is going to stop. Certainly the government do not know what expenditure this will run the country into, for neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Justice has been able to give us the least idea what our financial obligations will be under this convention. It does seem to me that the government of the day has resorted to the method of sending a representative of this country almost any place on God's earth, with almost unlimited power, to commit the government of this country to any expenditure, and then come back here with an agreement to which the government says, " hear, hear," and then asks this parliament to ratify it. It is treating this parliament with a certain degree of contempt. A resolution of this kind comes along, and this house is asked to ratify it when the government can give us no information at all regarding it. I would ask the Prime Minister, where is this going to stop? Are the limits even on the American continent or are they in Europe? It is absolutely impossible to my mind even to estimate what our financial obligations will be under this convention.
Again, why should we undertake all these obligations? It is quite true, as the hon. member for Port William (Mr. Manion) has pointed out, that some of these diseases are more or less common in this country, but the great bulk of them are not, and we are simply undertaking to police the world, so to speak, from a sanitary standpoint, to delouse the world, ships and everything else. We are simply asked to go forward blindfold and accept the responsibility of this undertaking. I do not know what powers were vested in Dr. Amyot when he went over there, but I certainly think they were much too wide when he comes back to this country with an obligation of this kind. I recall in 1920, when the present Prime Minister was then leader of the opposition, he wanted to

Convention-Mt. McGibbon
Sanitary
restrict the Prime Minister of that day as to what he should and should not do at the Imperial conference. But the whole attitude oi tills government seems to have changed. Having come back from the Imperial conference, they do not even ask parliament to ratify what they have done. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon argued that Mr. Lloyd George adopted a similar course when he was Prime Minister of Great Britain, and that consequently the parliament of Canada has no right to be consulted at all.
I wonder what has caused this change of heart on the part of the government. Is it due to the fact that we are a member of the League of Nations?-which I quite realize does not bring any comfort to the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice. Why are we asked to undertake obligations so foreign to the needs of this country when our national needs are absolutely neglected?
I am sorry that the Minister of Healtn (Mr. King) is not in his seat, for I intended to put some questions to him. I intended to ask him what his department has done to Tid this country of the grave narcotic evil. I have been trying to ascertain from the department, but I can get practically no information. And yet the narcotic habit, which every year is taking down thousands of our best citizens into an untimely grave or, what is worse, to debauchery, is increasing right under the very eyes of the Department of Health, but apparently they are oblivious to what is going on. I would say^ to the Prime Minister, if he wants my advice as a medical man, that he had better shake up his department, or it will discredit his government. Although the department has been in existence for some seven or eight years, I can say without fear of successful contradiction that it has done nothing to justify its creation; it is a dead letter throughout the country to-day so far as the preservation of the health of the nation is concerned. One of the specific purposes for which it was created was to deal with the soldier problem. What has it done in this respect? Practically nothing. It was also promised that there would be incorporated with it a department of scientific research-one of the most important branches of research under God's heaven in any government or any land. But what has it done? It has not even started to organize yet. To-day I do not believe that the Department of Health is doing anything more, or doing it any better, than heretofore was done by other departments of government. It seems to me that we have to go far afield, to undertake obligations which may

be far-reaching financially and otherwise, in order to give the department an excuse for existence.
Many extraneous subjects have been brought into this discussion. The Minister of Justice introduced the Locarno treaty, and also our status as one of the partners in the Britannic commonwealth of nations. He said he was equal to defending our position there; which is quite correct. But ask him what this country is doing to-day to help shoulder the burdens of empire now carried almost entirely by Great Britain, and there is no response. It is true that we are availing ourselves of all the protection accorded us by the Imperial authorities. Our complacent attitude in this respect always puts me in mind of the boy who has grown to manhood and still lives on his old father. That is what Canada is doing in relation to the mother country. In my opinion the time has arrived when we should shoulder our share of the necessary expense of the empire from which we are drawing very substantial benefits.
I also think that we might have participated in the Locarno treaty. I do not lay down the doctrine that we should bear any responsibilities where we are not consulted; but if Canada is in earnest in trying to preserve the peace of the world, we should do everything in our power to that end. As I said the other day, I think the Locarno treaty, if properly carried out, will do more to preserve world peace than anything that has been accomplished in the last four or five years. I recognize that we were not represented at Locarno, but I think we might have been. With Germany, France and Great Britain guaranteeing the European boundaries both east and west -Great Britain did not guarantee the eastern boundary; she said she could not be the policeman of the world, but she was willing^ to do so as far as she could. But to my mind the important feature of that treaty was that Germany herself guaranteed to protect those boundaries both east and west; and if she did that there could be no war between the nations concerned at least. I think if the spirit of Locarno had been carried out, if Great Britain, France and Germany had signed that treaty, it would have done more to preserve peace in Europe than anything else imaginable.
As a member of this house I object to undertaking obligations concerning which we know so little. We have not even been given an estimate of what this convention is going to cost Canada, or how far we shall be involved. I wonder if this convention is similar to the treaty we signed with Hungary and Turkey. When our accredited representatives signed

Sanitary Convention-Mr. Bennett
that treaty, and this house on the motion of the present Prime Minister endorsed it, and we were asked to say if we were going to stand by it, the government said we didn't know whether we were or not. Are all of our international agreements to be treated in that way? Here is a convention with certain reservations. How far are we involved; where are we going to stop? It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that the time is come when we must consider the revenues of this country as something not akin to an artesian well; we must recognize that there is a limit to the amount of taxation which we can collect, and I for one protest strongly against these unnecessary expenditures while our taxation is as high as it is to-day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended
to participate in this discussion. That it has wandered very far afield from the motion upon the order paper is quite apparent, and I think this is attributable to the explanations made by the Prime Minister as to how treaties should, might, could or would be signed.

The motion before the house is to approve of a convention entered into between certain countries at Geneva-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: At Paris.

At Paris; an international sanitary convention. My own personal view is that Canada would have been well-advised not to have touched the convention. I say that for this reason. We have here a federal union-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) touched upon the point-and the provinces are charged with the responsibility of public health, except where the Dominion deals with it by reason of sea ports or the international boundaries between us and United States. But even in the latter case, where health is concerned it has been the contention of the federal power that the provinces must be responsible for stamping out any epidemic within the provincial area. This convention is made between governments; the federal government of Canada, as a member of the League of Nations, is entering into a convention with other nations of the world. Clearly when Canada undertakes to
do certain things with respect to certain diseases, as to which under the constitution the provinces only have jurisdiction, this Dominion cannot exercise any power. The mere fact that the federal government signs a convention does not enable it to transgress the constitution of the country. This convention confers uo constitutional powers upon the federal government. The government's powers are just as they were before, and each of the provinces may be affected by outbreaks of the disease of smallpox, as mentioned. What power has this parliament to deal with smallpox? What power has this parliament ever exercised with respect to outbreaks of that disease? The provinces and the provinces only are concerned with the question of smallpox, and if an epidemic of smallpox should break out in Quebec or in Alberta the province of Quebec or the province of Alberta, as the case may be, must deal with it. The Dominion can do nothing at all in the matter. What is more, neither this parliament nor this government has the right under the constitution to impose upon any provincial government the necessity of making any return to the Minister of Health that sits yonder.
Had I been asked whether or not in my opinion we should become a party to the convention, I would have said. Certainly not. What purpose does it serve? I do fear-and I put this to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-that we in this country are beginning to think that because Canada is a member of the League of Nations it makes us appear to be important in the eyes of the world if we sign conventions and treaties. I regret to say this, but there is marked evidence of it. There is a jaunt across the water to Geneva. It is a lovely place and a delightful time is had. This country pays the expenses. There is excellent food on the ship and excellent provision is made for entertainment in Geneva and elsewhere. And then you must do something; you must sign a convention.

I said the food was excellent; I did not criticize it. All these entertainments are admirable, but in many instances they are holidays for those who participate in them. I do not say that it was a holiday for the Minister of Justice (Mir. Lapointe) when he went over in connection with

the question of naval disarmament-in respect of which, by t'he way, he nas not yet given a report to the house. That, I suspect, was not a holiday for him. But it has been a holiday for some of our representatives who have gone there. And, what is more, they were unable to participate in the proceedings of the League of Nations to the same extent as my hon. friend has done because of their lack of understanding and of appreciation of all that transpired.
Now here is a convention we are asked to approve. The ratification of a convention is, of course, as the Minister of Justice has said, a prerogative of the crown. The crown acts on the advice of its ministers, and in this instance the ministers from Canada will advise the crown that the convention is a sound one in which Canada concurs, if the Canadian parliament, comprising both the Commons and the Senate, approves of it. I wholly agree that it is desirable-indeed, I have always so held-that both the Commons and the Senate of parliament should be asked to approve of conventions or treaties that carry international implications or responsibilities. That, I think, is clear. When we are asked, as the Commons house of parliament, to give our approval to this convention, I submit that it is abundantly clear that we should not seek to commit the Dominion to do something with respect to the provinces which the Dominion has no constitutional jurisdiction to do. And clearly that is what is implied here; there is no escaping that conclusion if this means what it says. For that reason therefore, I would have said, with respect to a matter of this kind, "We are entirely of the opinion that there is no necessity for us to become a party to this convention ", That, I suggest, would have been the proper attitude for the Canadian representatives to have taken. I repeat, I see in all the proceedings of the League of Nations, so far as this country is concerned, an increasing evidence as the days go by of a desire on our part to find a place in the sun by signing conventions and treaties, thus suggesting that we have become a very important people. Importance in the world is not measured, I submit, in any such manner.
I go a step further. Some discussion has arisen with respect to the League of Nations. What is the League of Nations? The League of Nations is a covenant between various peoples that they will do certain things named in that covenant. Each of the contracting parties has incurred obligations, one of which is to enforce sanctions in the event of any member of the league violating the provisions of the covenant. That involves economic
UVIr. Bennett.]
sanctions and, if necessary, military sanctions as well. The Canadian people, then, have obligated themselves if necessary, so far as the League of Nations is concerned, to become parties with other nations to the enforcement of economic and, if needs be, of military pressure to 'carry out the will of the league.
Now what is the difference between the League of Nations and the British commonwealth of nations? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has been speaking in terms of war. The League of Nations involves in its very essence the exercise of military power, if needs be, for the purpose of giving effect to its will as against a transgressing member. That is all that can be said regarding it. The British commonwealth of nations is made up of a very large number of self-governing communities as well as of crown colonies and mandated territories in various portions of the world's area, embracing a quarter of it altogether. It is perfectly true that when Great Britain goes to war this country is also at war. It is equally true that this country need not participate in any such war unless this parliament sanctions our participation. That is clear. We have provided that by statute.
The hon. gentleman considers, then, that the statement made in South Africa recently is not well founded?

I do not believe that any lawyer thinks for a moment that it is well founded. With all deference to Mr. Hertzog, who is an eminent lawyer-as I think the Minister of Justice will agree-it is not possible for any portion of the empire to be neutral while the empire is at war. That is clear. If, however, his meaning was that any part of the empire comprising a self-governing dominion need not participate in that war, the statement is correct, inasmuch as it is for the parliament of that self-governing dominion to determine what action shall be taken. I do not think there can be much doubt about that in the light of all that has been written on the question and with which we are familiar. There can be no doubt about it in view of the statements that are made from time to time, not only by British but by Canadian statesmen as well, notably by the great leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that when Great Britain was at war Canada was at war. That was the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and it cannot be successfully disputed.
The position, then, with respect to the League of Nations and the British commonwealth of nations, is not wholly analogous We have become parties to the League of

Sanitary Convention-Mr. Bennett
Nations by a covenant which we have signed. A covenant is an agreement under seal. We have incurred certain obligations under the League of Nations and in the event of transgression on the part of any member that has signed the covenant, that member may be brought to book by the concerted effort of all the other signatory members including Canada, with economic sanctions and military power if needs be.
On the other hand, the British commonwealth of nations is a group of self-governing countries, including Great Britain; and under our system of government-under the system that has evolved through time and under which we now live-if Great Britain goes to war we are at war. But we are not compelled, as we are under the covenant of the League of Nations, to make contribution either of a dollar or of a man except in so far as we may decide to do so. This parliament having given its sanction to the covenant of the League of Nations, we are bound by that covenant- whatever we may think of it-to give effect to any decision it may arrive at for the purpose of enforcing its will against a transgressing member.
This convention is alleged to have for its object the preservation of peace, and that enables one to make some reference to the Locarno treaty. That also was intended to preserve peace, but this government thought it undesirable to be a party to that treaty. It will be recalled, with reference to the policy of Locarno, that the report of the Imperial conference of 1926 contained these words:
It then became clear that, from the standpoint of all the dominions and of India, there was complete approval of the manner in which the negotiations had been conducted and brought to so successful a conclusion. Our final and unanimous conclusion was to recommend to the conference the adoption of the following resolution:
"The conference has heard with satisfaction the statement of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs with regard to the efforts made to ensure peace in Europe, culminating in the agreements of Locarno; and congratulates His Majesty's government in Great Britain on its share in this successful contribution towards the promotion of the peace of the world."
I do not think any person unacquainted with the subleties of mind of hon. gentlemen opposite would conclude anything but that this parliament had given its approval, or at least that the government had given its approval, to the Locarno treaty; because when you find a gentleman saying that it is clear from the standpoint of all the dominions and of India that there has been complete approval of the manner in which the negotiations have been conducted and brought to a successful conclusion, followed by congratulations for
the results obtained, it shows, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) remarked, a desire to make it plain that there is complete unanimity on the part of Australia, New Zealand, Canada and South Africa as to the Locarno treaty. That is the attitude it is desired to express in England, while in Canada they wish to make it appear that they will not make any promises which will involve this country in anything beyond the three mile limit.
