speechtext: I was going to say to my hon. friend that I think he is entirely wrong on that point, and I would like to give him my reasons later.

I do not know that it rests with me to give my right hon. friend permission to do that. The rules of the house are there and I cannot change them. As far as I am concerned, if the right hon. gentleman has the right to speak he can do so, and if he has not that right he should not speak. Unfortunately I cannot add to that or take away from it. However, I cannot be wrong with respect to this; under our constitution, if we were to have an outbreak of smallpox, an epidemic, in one of the western provinces, the obligation rests with the provincial rather than with the Dominion government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will read the convention he will see that he is entirely wrong in believing that the provincial authorities have that obligation; under the exclusive jurisdiction given this parliament, we have to deal with matters of quarantine, navigation and the like, and those are the matters primarily referred to in this convention.

I was very anxious to
satisfy myself on that point, and the Prime Minister is quite correct in drawing attention to the fact that this parliament has power only to deal with questions of quarantine and with ships and shipping. But the
convention deals with cars and railways passing international boundaries. I will turn up the section if my friend desires; it deals with crossings between the United States and Canada, and under those circumstances there is no jurisdiction on the part of this parliament to deal with an epidemic of smallpox in Alberta. They may deal with the trains and with the passage of the trains, but they have no power to compel the province of Alberta to make any report to this Dominion in respect to an outbreak of smallpox; and until you amend the constitution you will have no power to do that, because matters of health rest wholly with the local authorities, as we have found out in times past in appeals on these very matters. The minister may sit here and make suggestions, but the provinces need not act upon them. This is not a matter on which the Dominion has concurrent powers. It has exclusive powers of quarantine, but this parliament has no power over a province in respect to smallpox.

May I ask a question?
Would not this parliament have power to deal with the matter to prevent the spread of smallpox from one province into another?

The courts have held to the contrary. That is the reason this parliament had no authority to deal with the epidemic of typhoid in Montreal and prevent it from spreading into Ontario, beyond the questions which I have pointed out, subject to the reservation as to the passing of interprovincial trains, et cetera, where the Dominion would have power to deal with this matter. There will come an opportunity later to discuss the question as to the powers of those who represent Canada either at Tokyo or at Washington or elsewhere; but the statement made by the hon. member from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) is a very careful and accurate statement of the situation. He had not his notes before him at the time but they are now in my hand, and the letter of Sir Esme Howard to the Secretary of State of the United States, dated June 24th, 1924, says:
The handling of matters at Washington exclusively relating to the Irish Free State should be confided to a minister plenipotentiary accredited to the United States government.
And that the Irish minister-
*-would be furnished with credentials which would enable him to take charge of all affairs relating only to the Irish Free State. He would be the ordinary channel of communication with the United States government on these matters. Matters which are of imperial concern or which affect other dominions in the commonwealth in

Sanitary Convention-Mr. Bennett
common with the Irish Free State will continue to be handled as heretofore by this embassy.	,
The arrangements proposed by His Majesty's government would not denote any departure from the principle of the diplomatic unity of the empire. The Irish minister would be at all times in the closest touch with His Majesty's ambassador, and any question which might arise as to whether a matter comes within the category of those to be handled by the Irish minister or not would be settled by consultation between them. In matters falling within his sphere the Irish minister would not be subject to the control of His Majesty's ambassador, nor would His Majesty's ambassador be responsible for the Irish minister's action.
I have been instructed to expess the hope that the United States government will concur in the appointment of an Irish Free State minister at Washington on the footing I have indicated above.
The United States Secretary of State in replying on June 28, 1924, notes that the Irish minister will have "the handling of matters at Washington exclusively relating to the Irish Free State", and that he will "take charge of all matters relating only to the Irish Free State." On December 7th, 1926, when the Hon. Mr. Massey was appointed, a question arose as to what his powers were, and his letter of credence issued on the day of his appointment shows that he was appointed "with the especial object of representing in the United States of America the interests of our Dominion of Canada." And when the Right Hon. Mr. Amery was questioned in the House of Commons as to the functions of the Canadian minister at Washington, he replied:
I would invite reference to statement of the Secretary of State, June 26. 1924, on the occasion of the appointment of the Irish Free State minister to Washington. The position is similar in the ease of the Canadian minister.
As to the powers of a Canadian minister in matters of the kind to which the Prime Minister has referred, and which have been mentioned by my friend, it is quite clear that they deal only with matters which affect Canada. Nothing better illustrates possibly the necessity of a clearer appreciation and understanding of any convention that is submitted to parliament than just what has taken place this afternoon. There are involved provincial rights; there are involved vast expenditures of public moneys, if this convention is approved. The ratification of it by necessary legislation will involve the amendment of the constitution of the country itself. It is necessary that those who represent us at the League of Nations should be advised that in matters such as this it is inadvisable that Canada should participate, because of our federal constitution, and due to
[Mr. Bennett.l
our peculiar position, differing from Australia and New Zealand, in relation to the United States to the south of us. And if we follow the course which prudence would dictate and the law which governs in such a matter, we should not be a party to this convention; for certainly the reservations which are mentioned in this protocol do not cover, in my judgment, the point which should be covered if we are to avoid being charged with bad faith in the future, because it affects provincial rights in respect of which this parliament has no control.
This will close the debate if the right bon. the Prime Minister speaks.

Sanitary Convention-Mr. Mackenzie King
Ships which have had, or have a case of smallpox on board either during the voyage, or at the time of arrival, may be subjected to the following measures:
(1)	Medical inspection.
(2)	The sick shall immediately be disembarked and isolated.
(3)	Other persons reasonably suspected to have been exposed to infection on board, and who, in the opinion of the sanitary authority, or by a previous attack of smallpox, may be subjected to vaccination, are not sufficiently protected by recent vaccination, or to surveillance, or to vaccination, followed^ by surveillance, the period of surveillance being specified according to the circumstances, but in any event not exceeding fourteen days reckoned from the date of arrival of the ship.

Over which parliament has no jurisdiction and the provincial authorities have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not interrupt my hon. friend. It must be clear to hon. members that the great purpose of this convention is to deal with diseases that are communicable through agencies of transportation and particularly agencies of transportation overseas. It is to prevent plagues and other communicable diseases from spreading from one country to another. Practically all of the sections relate to different diseases which may be carried from one place to another by infected ships. They are such diseases as the bubonic plague, smallpox, typhus, cholera and the like. Those are all referred to in the section.

Are the quotations which the Prime Minister has made not all under section 4 on page 8. "measures at marine ports and frontiers," while the other sections apply to other than marine ports and frontiers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The sections which I have quoted are all sections which apply to this country under this convention, and it is only the federal government which can take action on these matters of inspection at ports in the manner which the convention describes.
But section 6 deals with the land frontiers between the United States and Canada. .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would again submit that we have a federal Department of Health which was instituted for the very purpose of dealing with these matters of health that are likely to be of concern to the entire Dominion and every province would have a right to expect that the Dominion would cooperate with it in every possible way to prevent the spread of diseases of the character in question. May I say that when one takes into consideration the trade of Canada, expanding as it is towards all ports of the world, and the fact that this treaty is signed by such countries as Japan, China, India, there is the strongest of reasons why we in this parliament should be anxious to become a party to a convention of this kind. It places obligations upon those oriental countries immediately to notify other countries that are parties to the convention of any outbreak of disease which may occur in their ports and which may be communicated in the course of transit of a ship from one part of the world to another. If it were for no other reason than that of protecting our own people from disease this convention should be welcomed by this parliament.
My attention has just been drawn to section 132 of the British North America Act which provides:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
That does not cover this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend might there say that we have again a question of interpretation of what is and what is not the British Empire. I hope he will be able to see that under that clause the last vestige of his argument fades awray.

It has no relevancy to
this.

speechtext:
With respect
to the advisability and desirability of this country associating itself with other countries, particuarly those countries with which it is

trading, in an endeavour to prevent the spread of such frightful national plagues as cholera, smallpox, typhus and the like may I say a further word. If there were not even an advantage to Canada itself, there is I think an obligation upon our Dominion as a country to co-operate with other countries of the world in a humanitarian endeavour of this kind. Much has been said about furthering movements that will make for peace. The other evening we had a long discussion of that subject and on the importance of cultivating the international mind as a means of bringing about a better understanding between nations. I do not agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that Canada should not be represented at. these national conferences. I think as a nation we should take our share with the other nations of the world in helping to further those movements which make for greater international security and greater international goodwill.
I did not say that Canada should not be represented at an international gathering.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But that was the inference I gathered, or perhaps it was from remarks that were made by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) who took rather strongly the position that in some of these matters we should not be represented.
I beg the Prime Minister's pardon. I took no such position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will come
back then to the leader of the opposition who I think did use words to the effect that, because Canada was a member of the League of Nations, she was taking herself very seriously and felt that as a nation she should participate in all these national conventions and sign them.

I said that it was our
duty to attend once we became a member, but I said that there was no reason why, to make ourselves great, iwte should sign conventions; that was not a test of our greatness.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This convention relates to the important matter of disease in which this country is vitally interested. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) spoke about contradictory attitudes, but I think his own speech betrayed his own contradictory attitude, because the first part of it denounced us for assuming fMr. Mackenzie King.]
obligations and the latter part of it reprimanded us because we were trying under a special clause to evade some of the obligations.
Apart, however, from any of the particular points of discussion, viewing generally and broadly the wisdom of inviting parliament to consider the approval of treaties, might I say this further word in conclusion . in regard to the matter of bringing conventions and treaties to this parliament for approval. I submit that the day has passed when any government or executive should feel that they should take it upon themselves without the approval of parliament, to commit a country to obligations involving any considerable financial outlays or active undertakings. In all cases where obligations of such a character are being assumed internationally, parliament itself should be assured of having the full right of approving what is done before binding commitments are made. I would not confine parliamentary approval only to those matters which involve military sanctions and the like. I feel parliamentary approval should apply where there are involved matters of large expenditure or political considerations of a far-reaching character. As the Minister of Justice has said, a better example could not be given than that with respect to a possible treaty between the United States and Canada on the St. Lawrence waterway development. This government, should it be in office at the time that a treaty of the kind is being negotiated, has always had the intention of submitting it to parliament and of having it understood in advance that all negotiations involved the submission to parliament of any such treaty. It should now be understood that approval by parliament will be expected and necessary before that treaty, if it ever should come into being, would in any way bind this country. I say that this is a wise doctrine to follow in regard to all treaties irrespective of their particular character wherever they involve large national obligations.

I wonder if the
Prime Minister would give information on the point I raised as to whether the federal authorities feel they have jurisdiction in a matter of this kind to bring forward legislation implementing this convention, and that there will be no difficulties with regard to the provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I think the government has full authority for all it has agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that it is now six o'clock, because I shall have something to say in regard to the matter the hon. gentleman is now raising.

On April the 10th the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr.- Bennett) raised a question of privilege in connection with the release of one Baldy Robb, and his statement is to be found in Hansard at pages 1872 and 1873. I do not wish to re-open the debate, and I reiterate that such matters should not be discussed in the house.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member for West Calgary stated:
I had no communication with the Solicitor General with respect to this matter. I made no recommendations of any kind regarding the release of this convicted criminal; I left the responsibility where it belonged.
My hon. friend's memory is not accurate. He did have communications with me on two different occasions-
That is untrue.

-once in Ottawa and once in Montreal, and moreover his interview with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) was reported to me by the latter. I wish to declare now, as I did on March 29th last, that the hon. member's action in this matter does not cast any reflection upon his character as a public man or as a private citizen, but was dictated by a high sense of duty.
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair.
Just what I thought, an absolutely untrue statement.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the 29th of March I was absent from the house-
Louder.

I find it difficult to speak much louder, my throat being somewhat sore. On that occasion a statement was made with respect to Baldy Robb during the course of a discussion, and the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was warned by the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) that the leader of the opposition-referring to myself -would be able to give certain information as to the release of Baldy Robb. I leave it to this house to imagine what would have been the effect of that " warning " had the matter been left just as it then was.

This is a -question of
privilege?

Surely. But fortunately the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), followed the matter up and the Solicitor General then made certain other observations. In his statement to-day he says that he repeated what he had said on the previous occasion, that there was no reflection on the leader of the opposition as a public man. Let me quote his words:
-that the hon. member's action in this matter does not east any reflection upon his character as a public man or as a private citizen, but was dictated by a high sense of duty.
Why there should have been any necessity on the part of the Solicitor General to give his so-called warning in respect of such action I am unable to say. Last Tuesday X gave an explanation in respect of the matter, and yesterday the Solicitor General told me that he had read it. He added that he had had a conversation with me once in Mr. Robb's office when we were discussing pension matters and on another occasion in the Windsor hotel in Montreal in reference to Baldy Robb. To-day he sent me a copy of the statement he proposed to make, and I despatched a note to him stating that surely
Privilege-Mr. Bennett

he did not desire to say that I had had any communication with him as to this man. I was very careful in the statement I made to the house on Tuesday to use the word " communication ", because last session there was a great deal of discussion about Baldy Robb and considerable levity throughout the house in connection with the case, and I could not be certain whether or not I had had any conversation with any particular person in respect to it. Fortunately I find that on February IS, 1927, when speaking on the Atha-baska election inquiry, I made reference to the matter and stated my position. I said that the man was not entitled to a ticket of leave, that the Minister of the Interior had made certain statements, and that while I oould quite understand that he sympathized with the accused in the matter and had mentioned it to the Solicitor General, in the end the law officers of the crown must accept responsibility for whatever action they might take. I continued-and I am quoting from page 309 of last year's Hansard:
I remember distinctly the ease of Baldy Robb and two others being spoken to during the fall. I recall an expression of my own opinion with respect to the matter to the effect that it was important that an example be made. It is far more important-this is the attitude I took . that the law should be vindicated, though not vindictively, and that its majesty be upheld than that feelings of sympathy should prevail in relation to any individual. We have all experienced those things; every man in public life knows that he has to make the choice between sympathy and public duty. His sympathies naturally impel him to do what the bon. member from Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) rose in his place to-day and so admirably stated-"I signed a petition for the parole of these two prisoners, for the reason that my sympathy found expression in the act". _ That was done to change and mould the opinion of the Solicitor General and of the Minister of Justice favourably towards the request. But as a public servant, owing a duty to the public, it is not open to any public man occupying a position of trust to sign any petition for the release of any prisoner under a system of ticket-of-leave.
When yesterday the Solicitor General reminded me that he had had a conversation with me in the office of the Minister of Finance on an occasion when we were dealing with the pension bill and certain amendments which I desired to move to it, which the Minister of Health (Mr. King), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and he himself were considering, I turned up the journals of the bouse and found that the third reading of the bill was discussed on April 13, 1927. I have no recollection of that conversation; but I do not say for a moment that a casual conversation with respect to Baldy Robb did not take place during that

discussion. Nor do I say, although I have no memory of it, that the Solicitor General and I may not have spoken about the case in the Windsor hotel at Montreal. But I do not regard that, nor do I think would any hon. member, as a communication made to the Solicitor General with regard to leniency to be extended to Baldy Robb. However, I did state very distinctly in the house on Tuesday, in order that there might be no misapprehension, that I had said to the Minister of the Interior-to the Minister of the Interior, mark you-that I did not propose to criticize the action of the government if they released Baldy Robb. I never desire to escape responsibility for anything I have said. I gave the minister my reasons, although just prior to that I was under the impression that Baldy Robb was out on ticket of leave, and had so read in the newspapers.
The Solicitor General stated in the house this afternoon:
My friend's memory is not accurate. He did have communication with me on two different occasions, once in Ottawa and once in Montreal,-
I abject to his language. I am not going to say whether there were any conversations or not. If there were, they were casual conversations, not communications. I had no interview with him in regard to the case, nor did I discuss it with any member of the government save the Minister of the Interior. The Minister of the Interior bore me out in that last Tuesday. I repeat, he is the only one with whom I had any discussion on the subject.
Since recess I understand that the word "communication" is used by the Solicitor General and other lawyers in the province of Quebec in the sense of conversation.

It is used that way in the
dictionary.

Quite so; but we do not use it in that way. In my statement on Tuesday I referred to my "communications" with the minister, and then I added that I "stated" to the Minister of the Interior so and so. That is the distinction I was drawing at the moment. I went further; I said:
I made no recommendations of any kind regarding the release of this convicted criminal; I left the responsibility where it belonged. I did state, however, that I would not criticize any action that might be taken in the circumstances by the law officers of the crown.
That is, I made no recommendations involving my placing communications on the files of the department with respect to Baldy Robb, and I could not do so after the speech

Privilege-Mr. Bennett
I had made in the house in February last year. Had the Solicitor General used the word "conversation"-and I think he might have done so-instead of "communication" I would have no objection to the statement that he has made; I am not prepared to challenge him when he says that he had a conversation with me, if that term is to be applied to casual observations about Baldy Robb, for I fancy there are at least twenty-five or thirty hon. members who last session had conversations with respect to Baldy Robb. In fact the case was treated with considerable levity and there was a good deal of joking as to when he would get out of the penitentiary. When it was announced in the papers that the convict had been released, I thought he was at liberty up to the time when the Minister of the Interior in his office told me that this was not so.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that I had no communications with the Department of Justice with respect to this man, and that I made no recommendations. If the casual conversations that took place between not only the Minister of the Interior and myself but with dozens of other hon. members with respect to Baldy Robb are to be termed "communications", then the Solicitor General's statement is correct; but those casual conversations were not so treated by me, and in my observations last Tuesday I was very careful to draw a distinction between what I regard as a communication and the statement which I said I made to the Minister of the Interior. I have no apologies to offer for my attitude in this case first, last and all the time, but I do resent keenly the covert suggestion that there was something wrong about my action, that the member for West York had to be warned, when the "warning" turned out to be nothing more than that I had done my duty as a public servant, that in fact there was no reflection on me one way or the other. I do not think that that was the intention of the so-called warning, and fot that reason I have risen to vindicate myself. I resent most strongly the suggestion that I had communication with members of the government for the purpose of securing the release of Baldy Robb. As the Minister of the Interior very frankly and very honestly said on Tuesday, I left that responsibility where it belonged. I told him that I was perfectly willing not to criticize any action the government might take upon a proper realization of the circumstances, that is, that they should be governed by the opinion of the judge and the warden of the penitentiary.

Mr. Speaker, on the question of
privilege, I wish first to congratulate my hon. friend on the tone which he has adopted this evening. It is a welcome change from the attitude which he took at recess. As to the word "communication", in justification of myself I may say that before using the word I was careful to look it up in the dictionary.
That makes it worse.

And this is what the word "communication" means - Murray's New English Dictionary, volume two, page 700:
Communication: the imparting, conveying, or exchange of ideas, knowledge, information, etc., whether hy speech, writing, or signs. Interchange of speech, conversation, conference, converse, personal intercourse.
In Webster's New International Dictionary, at page 452:
Communication:	(2) intercourse by words
letters, or messages; interchange of thoughts or opinions, by conference or other means; converse; correspondence; (3) that which is communicated or imparted; intelligence; news, a verbal or written message.
Therefore I contend that I was perfectly justified in stating that there had been communications from the leader of the opposition to myself in connection with the matter. The hon. gentleman has mentioned a note which he sent over. In fairness to myself and in fairness to the house I think that the note should be quoted as sent. And this is the note:
The Solicitor General: Surely you do not mean that I ever sent you any "communication" regarding Robb. You must mean "conversation". I -was very careful to say "communication". R.B.B.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would simply ask my hon. friend to explain why he was so careful to use the word "communication" if he wanted to exclude conversations, when, in the paragraph before that relating to myself, he quoted a conversation with the Minister ot the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton). Why should conversations with the Minister of the Interior be relevant and conversations with myself have nothing to do with the matter? I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is good thing that this incident should close now, and again I congratulate the leader of the opposition upon having adopted to-night a tone which is by far more in keeping with the very high position he occupies in the house than was the tone he adopted this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, seeing that I seem to have been the central spirit in this discussion, may I make it very clear to the house, as I think I did on a
Privilege-Mr. Bennett

former occasion, that I have no interest in Baldy Robb. Indeed, if my interests had been consulted perhaps they would have been best served by leaving him where he was. But being in receipt of a very largely signed petition from people in the province of Alberta, and being asked in that petition to take action, I did so. I want to say here and now, however, that never at any time had I any interest in this prisoner such as I would not take in any other prisoner in the province of Alberta. I make this statement because the inference might go abroad that I was the person in this house who was going about interviewing people on behalf of Baldy Robb. That I never did. As a matter of fact I have suffered more at his hands than I have on account of any other person in that province. I bear no ill-will in the matter, however. I was perfectly willing to do what I could to meet the request contained in the petition, just as I should do for any other prisoner. But, I repeat, I have no interest in the individual.

The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) was good enough to ask me a question, which I think I may answer in the terms of Hansard itself. I do not wish to quote too much of what I said the other day, but I may read the following:
It transpired that the minister was correct and we had some conversation touching the matter.	My recollection is that I stated I
would have nothing to do with it, pointing out, however, that I had recently been in Edmonton where I had learned that a large number of people there, who had been associated with the prosecution of Robb, were of the opinion that the ends of justice had been satisfied and the law vindicated by his conviction and imprisonment, and that, having regard to the fact that his wife and family were in poor circumstances, there was no reason why, if the government deemed it a proper course to pursue and such a recommendation should be made to His Excellency, Baldy Robb should not be released on tieket-of-leave. If I remember rightly the Minister of the Interior inquired whether I would have any objection to communicating that fact to the leader of the opposition. I told him I would not. I ascertained that the leader of the opposition was absent from Ottawa, as was also the Solicitor General, and I telephoned the Minister of the Interior to that effect.
I had no communication with the Solicitor General with respect to this matter. I made no recommendations of any kind regarding the release of this, convicted criminal; I left the responsibility where it belonged. I did state, however

I emphasize that.
__that I would not criticize any action that
might be taken in the circumstances by the law officers of the crown. The view I intimated to the Minister of the Interior, the only minister with whom I had had any discussion with reference to the question.

Those are the facts. Casual convensations with regard to Baldy Robb certainly were not discussions concerning him, and the only discussion I had was with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton). If, however, casual conversations are to be regarded as discussions, then it is a warning to me in the future, with respect to at least one of the law officers of the crown.

speechtext:
While discussing the question of reports, may I say that last night my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) directed the attention of the house to the fact that he, as well as other hon. members, had through some inadvertence failed to receive the report of the joint engineering board on the St. Lawrence waterway project. I have made inquiries as to what took place with regard to the distribution of the report and I find, as I intimated yesterday, that the report is in two volumes. It is rather bulky and includes a number of expensive plates. The actual cost of publication of the report is 812.50 for the report and plates. At the time of its receipt the government did not have it distributed generally, although I understand, any members who had applied to the Department of Railways-not to the distribution office-were supplied with copies. Some hon. members, however, seem to have been under the impression that the report was being distributed through the distribution office, and not having received copies there were naturally surprised. I may observe that copies are available for all members of the house, but those gentlemen who have already received copies from the Department of Railways will not expect additional copies unless for some special reason. Any members who so desire may receive a copy of the report on application. When the report was laid on the table of the house it was distributed to the leading newspapers throughout the country, to the universities, the provincial governments and a number of leading libraries as well as engineering journals and societies. It has been made available at a nominal cost of $5 to the members of the engineering profession, and indeed to any person interested in it for professional reasons. It was not thought advisable to distribute a report of that magnitude and cost free of charge, and the government will maintain the nominal charge of $5 for a report which has cost it $12.50 to print.
I have just one other observation to make. The report has been printed at the expense 56103-126
of the department, but it has not been translated into French. I think it should be translated; I believe it should be made available to all members of parliament and I hope the committee on public printing of this house will consider the advisability of the tran. slation and publication of this report in French.

Sections 1 to 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Sale, etc., of clovers, grasses, seed grain and fodder seeds.
Has the minister considered whether or not section 4 as contained in this bill is a legal and valid section?
Yes.
Do the law officers say it is valid?
I presume it is.

As I said the other day, I do not wish to raise questions of this kind unnecessarily, but I think it my duty to point out the fact that there are grave questions connected with a statute of this parliament which forbids any person having seed in his possession unless under certain conditions; that is a serious matter. This section states:
No person shall sell, offer, advertise, expose or have in possession for sale for the purpose of seeding in Canada any seeds in containers containing seeds of clover, alfalfa, grasses, flax, sorghums, millet, wheat, oats, barley, rye, corn, buckwheat, sunflower, field peas, field beans, vetches, or other kinds of seeds that may be prescribed by regulation, nor shall any shipment be billed as seed unless each container containing such seed, or a tag or label durably attached thereto, is branded or marked on one side in printed characters ....
Certainly the powers of this parliament are very wide with respect to agriculture, but I cannot help thinking that the rights of the provinces are invaded in some degree by the provisions of that section. I am not expressing an opinion, but I think it should be submitted to the law officers before the bill is finally passed out of committee.

I realize that there is an element of doubt as to our jurisdiction, especially with regard to transactions between citizens of the same province. There are three kinds of sales; there is the sale for export, over which we have undoubted control; there
'Mr Ladner.]
is the interprovincial sale, which we also control, and there is the sale between persons in the same province. This has stood all the tests since 1911, so I think we are fairly safe in letting it go through again.
Is this a change from the existing regulations?
This is really one of the most important changes which has been made. Perhaps the chairman would read subsection (e).

speechtext:
There is quite an amount
of seed grain grown in British Columbia. What effect will this have upon people buying seed from one another?

The seeds will be
the same, but they will be of different names.
What about the regulations?

There are no
changes in the regulations yet. Regulations are never drafted until after the bill is adopted. That will come later.

They grow a great deal
of timothy seed up in the valley. If a man sells timothy seed to another man in a different part of the province, does that have to be graded?
There is no change in regard to timothy seed.

In regard to seed grain
in the province, will it have to come under the regulations?

No, no change
whatever. It is just in the nomenclature of the grades. The grades of seed are now 1, 2 and 3; the registered grades are' registered extra, registered No. 1 and registered No. 2; three grades in each. Nos. 1, 2 and 3, are commercial grades.

Seeds Act Amendment
As the statute now stands, it applies to all transactions whether inside or outside of the province?
Yes.

Whether it is legal or
not is another question; but as it stands it now applies to all, inside as well as outside of the province.
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to
me that this clause is going too far in establishing three more grades. Goodness knows we have enough grades already. There is another feature which I do not like. It provides for grades higher than 1, 2 and 3; the consequence is that a man going into a store to buy grass seed, the unscrupulous dealer, if there are such, says: Here is No. 1 grade, and quotes a price for it. The man naturally thinks that is the best grade, and the dealer does not tell him that there are three grades ahead of it. I think it is a great mistake to have fancy names. If there are six grades and a man is told that a certain seed is No. 6 grade, he knows what that is; but if it is No. 1, he thinks it is the best. It has always been a standing grievance that the government will put on "extra" and "fancy" grades ahead of No. 1 grade, which to the man on the street gives a false impression. If you must have six grades, I think they should run from one to six. I should like to know what would be the germination of the sixth grade.

The grades are not all registered. The grades 1, 2 and 3 are just seed, whether of wheat, oats or whatever it is; it is not aristocratic seed. But as to high class, registered seed, that is called now in the bill " registered extra," " registered No. 1 " and "registered No. 2." I think what my friend is getting at is why they are not called by corresponding names to the unregistered. That is at the request of the seed growers1 association, who have done a lot of useful work in western Canada. They do not like the idea of a registered No. 3; that is setting down too low when it comes to a high class registered grade. They suggest that it should be called "registered extra", "registered No. 1" and "registered No. 2". They avoided the 3. Personally I would rather have seen it registered No. 1, 2 and 3, to correspond to the other grades 1, 2 and 3.
Why does not the minister change it now?

I am following the rulings of the agriculture committee. I do not see in the house the farmers' repre-56103-126i
sentatives on that committee. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and myself were in the minority. If this committee thinks that is [DOT] the sensible thing to do, naturally I will be agreeable; but I would say that the agricultural committee wanted it in this way because of the successful work done by the seed growers.
What about the buyers of seed?
It is more understandable by them, and after all they are more numerous than the growers.
The buyers are the ones to protect, and you protect them better with this suggestion.

If anyone made the motion that the registered grades should be registered No. 1, registered No. 2 and registered No. 3, I would accept it. But remember that these parties have made a very strong bid for it the way it is. We are sacrificing convenience a good deal to meet the class of men who are doing extra work and think there is something in these names and do not like to adopt the standard No. 3 for seed.
As a matter of fact, the minister admits that in practice there is a No. 3, but it is called something else. We had better call it what it is.
I do not know whether my hon. friend would agree to that when it is applied to fruit.
It would apply to everything.

We like to get away
from the numerical grades 3 and 4.
While the seed growers' association represent the seller, do they to any extent represent the buyer?
Yes, that is right; the Canadian Seed Growers' Association naturally represent themselves.
They do not represent the buyers.

Oh, no doubt they sometimes buy from each other. The growers of registered stock sell back and forth to farmers; but those transactions are small in comparison with the purchases of the average man who is buying seed grain.

Mr. Chairman, I beg to move:
That subparagraph (e) of clause 5 be amended by striking out the word "extra", so that the clause will then read:

-in order to carry out the purpose of the section.

There are only two or three copies of the written amendment that was made in the agriculture committee. With the amendment now made it will read:
(2) For seed derived from an inspected seed crop that was pure as to variety and was registered by the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, registered No. 1, registered No. 2 and registered No. 3.

To the grade names registered No. 1 and registered No. 2 may be added such word or words as may be prescribed by regulation to describe any damage to the seed when such damage does not affect its seed value.

That has been

There are inspectors and seed laboratories at convenient points.
Will the minister have one in the northern part of British Columbia?

Along the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific?

On section 9-Power to change name.
If a registered name is granted to a seed grower, can that name be changed or cancelled without the seed grower being consulted?

The proper thing
to do would be to acquaint him of the fact that a change was contemplated and to give him an opportunity to justify the continuance of the name. For instance, if a variety name had been granted and the seed proved not to be living up to its name but to be merely developing into a strain of some other variety, such as marquis wheat or something like that, there would be no reason to continue the name; but in ordinary courtesy the seed grower should be notified and given an opportunity of proving that he was right and that the department was wrong. The advisory board and the department would be the final authority in the matter. The purpose of this is to correct any mistakes that have been made in the past in the matter of too much generosity in granting licenses for new varieties. We have been suffering from a plethora of varieties of grain, especially wheat.

I have in mind vermilion wheat. I am not going to say whether in my opinion it is a good or a bad wheat, but I understand that some question has arisen whether it is a good milling variety, and I believe a license was granted to the grower and later on was taken away from him without notice.
That would not be done. He would be given proper notice and an opportunity of defence.
What steps have been taken to determine whether or not a variety of grain or seed is valuable, and whether a variety should be given a name?

sample of it would be taken, preferably sealed and certified to as being of that variety. Mr. APRIL 12, 1928

Newman, the Dominion Cerealist, would then make a milling test and a baking test, and he would have it judged on its merits in that respect. The primary purpose for which we grow wheat is its value as a food.

On section 10-False advertising.

I should like to draw attention to the last part of this clause, which reads:
Nor shall cereal grains, grasses or clover seeds be advertised for sale unless the grade name is included in the advertisement.
Let us think what that means. Feed stores generally sell and advertise seed grain and grass seeds, and every time they put on their billhead or in their advertisement in a little monthly or weekly paper that they sell these things, they will have to put, in the case of clover, the fact that they are selling registered No. 1, registered No. 2, registered No. 3 and No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 grades. It is absurd that they cannot advertise the fact that they have for sale seed grain or grass seed without inserting the grade of every particular variety they have. That is wrong. If the intention is to prevent a person advertising one grade as another, that is all right, but it should be so expressed. This will prevent any man advertising, either on his billhead or in hi3 weekly paper, the fact that he sells grass seeds unless he names the grade of every one of the grass seeds he carries. If he carries ten kinds with six grades for each kind, his billhead will be filled up with this information.

Section 14 makes
four distinct exceptions to the application of this bill which I think will cover what my hon. friend has in mind. The farmer often has to sell a carload on the basis of grade after it is cleaned by the seed merchant. I have sold many carloads that way myself without any grading. We will let this section stand until we come to section 14.

speechtext:
This section has been amended to read:
Section thirteen of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:
No person shall import into Canada for the purpose of selling or offering for sale, or for the purpose of seeding, any of the seeds named in section five of this act, or any kinds of garden vegetable seeds that may be prescribed by regulation, unless they are branded or marked or coloured in accordance with the provisions of this act and conform to the regulations thereunder.
This seems rather a radical change. What is the explanation?	fl".

No, it is quite
simple. My hon. friend will note that it says "unless they are branded or marked or coloured." I do not know whether my hon. friend knows, but it is the usual practice in Canada and elsewhere to have a certain percentage of imported clover and alfalfa seed coloured. We rather like the idea, because it indicates which is Canadian seed that has a high reputation in other countries. The same conditions prevail with regard to identifying seeds in other countries.

Section agreed to.
On section 14.
We have not a copy of the bill as amended by the committee, Mr. Chairman.
It is not the usual practice to reprint the bill unless the changes made are very considerable.

I think much of this confusion is due to the facts that our new rules, of which we have heard something before, were amended last year to cut down largely the numbers on the agriculture committee, and the consequence is that half the members who are interested in farming now see this bill for the first time, whereas had there been the same number on the committee as in former years we would have been able to discuss this matter much more intelligently,
Seeds Act Amendment

and there would not have been all this confusion. That is one more thing to the credit of the beloved new rules.
Section 14 agreed to.
Section 15 agreed to.
On section 10-false advertising.

I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that section 14 does not refer in anyway whatever to section 10. It makes exemptions under sections 5, 6 and 7, but it does not in any way refer to section 10. I would draw the attention of the committee to the original section 10, which will be found on the opposite page of the bill, and which says, and very properly, that no person shall sell any seeds that are falsely represented in any advertising. That is perfectly proper, but that is not what the new section says. The new section says that you shall not advertise grains, grasses or clover seeds unless the grade name is included in the advertisement. I know something about this business because I have been in it for fifteen years, although out of it now, and I know that it is customary for people in this business to advertise that they are dealing in these things. They simply say that they have a supply of grains and grass seeds on hand, and there is no false description and no false advertising about it, but under this new section they are forbidden to put that simple advertisement on their billheads unless they specify every individual grade of seed, and there are six of every kind of seed which they handle. I know what the government is getting at, but it is not expressed correctly. It would be much better left as it was originally in the act.

If a seed man advertises so much grass, clover, wheat, oats or any other seed, how can the buyer make an intelligent bid unless he is told whether it is grade 1, 2, 3 or registered 1, 2, 3? It seems to me that at present there is plenty of room for fraud, unintentional perhaps; to advertise such and such seed in extravagant terms. If my hon. friend bought that seed, say a certain variety of clover, and found it below grade, he would be very much disappointed. That has been our experience in the administration of the Act.

The minister does not grasp my point. The old section covers what he has described. It made it an offence to falsely describe what you are offering for sale. Customers in the retail trade do not bid; they come in to buy and know what they are

getting. If they are buying No. 1, they see that they get No. 1. But this amendment refers to advertising. If I advertise No. 1 seed and supply No. 2 I am liable under the old act and can be punished. But now I have to be prevented from advertising by way of my bill head unless I set out a whole rigmarole of ten or more different kinds of seed, each of six grades. If anyone will take the trouble to read the old section on the right hand of the page he will see that the public is fully safeguarded against any fraudulent advertisement. If I advertised myself as a dealer in potatoes, would I have to describe the life history of each potato?

I have no seed
catalogue under my hand, but my experience is that every parcel of seed sold by a seed house is graded.
Certainly, but not advertised.

If that is so with the seed firm, then everyone who sells seed by advertisement should comply with the same conditions in order to give the prospective purchaser a chance to buy intelligently. If he does not know what he is getting, he is buying a pig in a poke. Suppose he is buying wheat, there is a tremendous spread between the best and worst grades. I think my hon. friend might look into this a little more thoroughly.
I have been looking into it for sixteen years.
This amendment is sought to remedy the injustice done to buyers of seed by reason of glowing seed advertisements in newspapers without any grade being specified.
That was fraudulent, and the old section covers it.
We are a party to the fraud if we do not close that open gate.

It seems to me that this section is badly drawn to accomplish what the minister has in mind. The objection taken by the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is well founded. If seed people advertise it would be entirely right for them to state in their advertisements that they have a stock of seed on hand for sale.
Hear, hear.

That is reasonable and business-like. You ought to arrange it so that when seeds are presented for sale the bags and packages shall show definitely what is being

Seeds Act Amendment
sold. As the hon. member for Comox-Albemi says, you should not require a man to advertise all the grades he has in stock. That is his point.
I do not think there is any abuse by the seed houses at all; their catalogues are before the whole country.
If that is the case, cut this out.

This is to cover the case of a person who inserts a short advertisement in the newspapers that he has such and such clover seed for sale at certain prices. I do not see how any prospective purchaser can buy that seed with any safety unless he knows what grade it is. If the committee thinks that the man who buys as a result of reading an advertisement should buy with his eyes shut as to the quality of the seed, we can leave the section in its original form. But I have some regard for the buyers; they are in the majority.
But you are prohibiting a man from advertising that he is a seed merchant.
I am prohibiting him from faking a prospective buyer by offering something, the quality of which is unknown.
Everybody agrees with that; but the section goes much further as it is worded.
Does my hon. friend think it better that the buyer should buy blindly?
Certainly not.
He would if the seed is not graded.
If the seed merchant is going to sell specific seed of specific quality he must comply with this act; but the section is broad enough to prevent his advertising at all.
Our whole grading system would be set at naught if we did not buy and sell by it.
The minister does not grasp the point.
It is simplicity itself. Let us dispense with grading; then wheat is wheat, clover is clover, grass seed is grass seed.

I gather from the member for Comox-Albemi that thousands of farmers throughout the Dominion buy their seed from
the small retail merchants. I sell car loads every year. This section would prohibit those merchants from advertising that they are simply selling seed unless they insert a whole
page ad. specifying the different qualities for sale. I do not see any sense in it.
There is none.
Is the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) referring to the small packages of seeds we see in every store?

No; in quantity. The retail merchant might buy a carload of clover or timothy seed for distribution in his locality. To sell that seed he has to advertise. But if he does so you compel him to advertise each and every grade that he has in stock. The member for Comox-Alberni contends that all he should be required to advertise is simply this: I have clover or timothy seed for sale. He should not be required to specify every grade. Surely the farmer knows enough to ascertain the grade when he buys seed.

I think this is a
decided safeguard for the buyer. If we prefer to legislate for the seller, then the buyer must look after himself. Which is the greater interest? All who favour legislation in this particular instance for the benefit of the seller will be in favour of eliminating it. I should prefer to legislate for the buyer. Joking aside, the primary object of the Seeds Act, the reason for its adoption twenty-five years ago, was after all to introduce a reasonable measure of fairness between buyer and seller, not only as regards home consumption, but as well for the protection of the buyer in Canada against spurious importations from abroad. I should not like to change this section offhand, but I am agreeable to having the bill stand in committee. Of course we all like to get our bills through, but I would rather have the bill stand than hurriedly change it.
Mt. MdMILLAN: I think you are trying to get the farmer to do the very thing that you say he should not do. When I go into a store to buy my seed I use my eyes, but the minister suggests that the farmer does not need to do so.

If the hon. member will second the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and accept the responsibility for what is done we can have the words in question eliminated. Or perhaps the committee would prefer to let the matter remain in committee. I want to be as amiable as possible to-night.
Seeds Act Amendment

It seems to me that the objection of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi would be met by a differentiation between advertising and selling. Leave advertising free from the application of this new clause.

That would meet my objection, but it would not be fair; it would not impose a penalty on people who falsely advertise. Why not strike out section 10 altogether, and have the old section 10 reinstated? That section reads:
No person shall sell, offer or have in possession for sale any seeds or plants that are falsely represented in any form of advertising.
That provision would cover the matter. I suggest that we leave out the section altogether and have that old provision put into effect.
There is a practice, particularly in the west, when advertising seed grain, grass seeds and clover seeds, to mention the price but not the grade.
How can you grade your grain in your granary? If it is in your granary and you advertise it for sale, how will you grade it?

The farmer cannot sell it until he gets the certificate of the Seed branch. We are not discussing commercial grain sold by the carload. In my opinion it would be a mistake to strike out the section, and I would therefore suggest that we leave the matter in committee and have the section redrafted so as to protect the buyer in the manner indicated, without giving offence to the seller in the way implied by my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi. The house in committee on Bill No. 170, to amend the Special War Revenue Act-Mr. Robb-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

When this bill was in committee on Tuesday evening every clause had been adopted, but it was proposed by the leader of the opposition, I think, that the bill be not taken out of committee until such time as we had considered a suggestion made by the hon. member for West York in regard to the manner in which we should proceed to make collections of sales tax. Before I deal with that I want to make one or two observations in explanation of certain questions raised on Tuesday. The leader of the opposition inquired as to how many cases of sales tax were
rMr. Motherwell.!
actually in the courts. I made the statement then that I thought there were between 500 and 600; I was quoting from a tabulated report. I was in error. To be exact, the number is 347-not so great as I thought at the time. There was also in the report in Hansard the statement that the amount of money which we expected to collect from brewers and distillers in oases now in the courts was half a million. As a matter of fact what I did say was, nearly five millions. A further question was asked by the leader of the opposition as to how many exemptions from sales tax had been passed by order in council. I said at the time that I thought there were none. I shall have to modify that slightly; there were a few. The roasting and grinding of coffee were exempted from the application of the sales tax for the reason that it was impracticable and unfair to apply it. The grocery stores were grinding and roasting coffee and were in competition with the ordinary roasters engaged in business on a large scale. We thought this was unfair and we made the exemption by order in council. Why?

For a number of reasons
One reason is that it will make the work of the department a great deal easier, and another is that it will save money to the department. For example, if a wholesaler who holds a license does not pay his sales tax when he buys from the manufacturer, or if he happens to have bought from the manufacturer and there is a reduction made in the sales tax, as happened this year and last year, the department losses the revenue from the reduction of the sales tax. Another reason is this: I take it that the theory of the application of the sales tax is that it should be applied as nearly as possible at the source, that is, the manufacturer or the importer, and that is the principle we would like to carry out. I would add that the wholesalers, through their organizations, waited upon the minister and made their representations, and I am informed that they are pretty well satisfied with the change. We are trying to make it as easy as possible; we are making it easy with regard to the taking of the stock as of June 30, and we are making it easy for them to pay the sales tax on the stock on hand. We are not asking for an immediate payment of the whole amount of the sales tax, but are permitting them to pay by instalments. I believe the change is in the interests of the department and I believe the method we are going to adopt now is the method which should have been adopted in the first place. I also believe the wholesalers will be quite satisfied, and in fact are now very well satisfied with the method we are going to adopt.

The minister has clearly stated the intention of the department, and July 1 is not very far away. I have received communications from wholesalers in various parts of the country indicating that it may work a very great hardship upon them to have these licenses cancelled as of July 1. It has been alleged also in some cases that political pressure was being brought to bear to secure the waiver of the operations of the prescriptive rule in the cases of some wholesalers and not in others.
