Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 54, to amend the Excise Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Minister may refuse or suspend license.

With respect to new
section 10, I desire to make a few observations. It will be remembered that the parliamentary committee had to investigate certain matters that involved the exercise by the executive of the powers contained in the former section which is now replaced by this new section. I need hardly point out that that was the cause of much abuse. There is given to a minister a power that no single man should exercise politically. Although one may entertain the highest possible opinion of the present minister or his successors or predecessors, the fact remains that the government have made it possible, for purely political reasons, to work a very serious and great hardship upon the public revenues by showing on the one hand favouritism and partiality or, on the other, vindictiveness. The evidence before the special committee was very clear upon that matter and it is very clear to any thoughtful member. The proposed new section reads:
The minister may for any reason which he deems sufficient in the public interest refuse to issue any license or to grant any privilege authorized by this act, or may suspend, cancel or revoke a license granted or any privilege given by this act.
Without appeal, with the mere assertion that it is in the public interest, the minister may suspend or cancel a license. The old section was open to the same objection. The evidence before the committee clearly indicated that the moment there was a violation of the law and the department desired to cancel the license which could not then be renewed, the pressure of political friends became so insistent that, however willing the minister might be to discharge his plain duty, he was in many instances overborne by the pressure of that political influence. The converse also was true; that where you found those engaged in the business opposed to the administration of the day and there was a possible breach of the law, the pressure of political friends against that political opponent to break down his business by cancelling the license was very great. The cases we had before us were clear. Obviously, of course, they did not say that that was the reason for doing this. I suggest that there should be

a power of review. It is not right that in the hands of a minister such a power should rest, nor should it be a purely political power. It must be remembered that that is a punishment of the most severe character. It destroys the business of the person concerned. That is not the prerogative of government. It rests with the courts awarding sentences, fines-and penalties, to carry into effect that punishment which follows an infraction of the law; but the punishment here is to destroy the man's business, and it may be done. I am perfectly frank; I say to the minister that I do not think he would do it, but I also say that he might do it without knowing he was doing it. Not that the minister is in any sense lacking in astuteness, but the exigencies of political necessities in cases such as I have had occasion to observe may result in that end being attained, although the reason given for it will be a very high-sounding one, and in the public interest, of course, in the noblest sense of the term. We have heard of these things happening before. I suggest that this section should be reconsidered. If it were as it stood originally I intended to speak to it, because it was quite clear before our committee that this section placed in the hands of the minister a power dangerous alike to the subject and the crown, and I think it should not be there without the right of appeal.

The bill as now printed, which is I believe in the hands of members, is somewhat different from the bill as introduced into this house and given its first reading. After the bill was given its first reading, certain representations were made, some from western Canada, asking for other amendments to the Excise Act, and we thought that we should make those changes. I therefore propose to move certain amendments as we proceed, introducing these other changes, but they have already been incorporated in the bill which is now known as Bill No. 54. What is now the first section of the bill was not in the bill as originally introduced.

It was not in the bill
when it was given its first reading?

No. I move, Mr. Chairman, that the following be inserted as section 1 of the bill:
1. The said act is amended by inserting after section nine thereof the following section:
9a.	(1) The rates and duties of excise
imposed by this act or any other law relating to excise as well as the rates and duties of excise heretofore imposed by any law' relating to excise or inland revenue enacted and in force since the first day of July, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven, shall be binding and are declared and shall be deemed to have been always binding and payable by His Majesty in

Excise Act Amendment
respect of any goods which may be hereafter or have been heretofore manufactured or imported by or for His Majesty, whether in the right of His Majesty's government of Canada or His Majesty's government of any province of Canada, and whether or not the goods so manufactured or imported belonged at the time of manufacture or importation to His Majesty; and any and all such acts as aforesaid shall be construed and interpreted as if the rates and duties of excise aforesaid were and are by express words charged upon and made payable by His Majesty. _ Provided, however, that nothing herein contained is intended to impose or to declare the imposition of any tax upon, or to make or declare liable to taxation, any property belonging to His Majesty either in the right of Canada or of a province.
(2) Without restricting the generality of the foregoing when any goods subject to excise have been seized or forfeited by His Majesty's government of any province in Canada or any public authority established by or under the authority of any such government, the duties of excise imposed by this act shall be payable and may be recovered in the same manner as if the said goods were found in the possession of any private person.
I might explain that this amendment arises out of legislation which has been passed by one of the provinces giving the province the power to go into the business of distilling liquor. There is some doubt whether when a province does that, the Dominion government has the right to impose excise taxes and we just want to make sure that we can collect excise taxes on liquors whether the liquor is made by private manufacturers or by the province. I think the committee will see the reasonableness of that amendment.
Mr. BENNETT; Does this refer to brewing and distilling?
To collecting the excise taxes [DOT]on the distilling of liquor.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-Minister may refuse or suspend license.

This is the section to
which I was speaking, which was section 1 in the bill as originally introduced. My hon. friend from North Simooe has made a suggestion which I think would do much to meet that difficulty, and that is to amend it to read that the minister may, in the case of [DOT]conviction, do so and so.
For violation of the act?

Yes. That at least involved a fair court trial and determination *of guilt before the minister acts, and to that [DOT]extent releases the minister, it seems to me,
from unfair pressure at least at the inception, because first there must be a conviction. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for North Simcoe would go a long way to meet the situation, and is not unreasonable.

I do not see any particular objection to that. Without casting any reflection upon any of the brewers or distillers, I think possibly in most cases that would give the minister power to suspend or cancel the license.
At least it would give them warning that that power was there for use in the future.

I think the committee should realize that the criticism of the leader of the opposition is directed just as much against the bill as it was originally introduced as it is against the amendment before us because under the bill as originally introduced the department or the minister had the power to refuse to renew the license at the end of the year, on March 31st. The hon. leader of the opposition has stated that that is an extreme power to put into the hands of the minister, and that it might be used for political reasons.
I said, because of the pressure of political friends.

I do not like to admit that such a thing could possibly happen. I hope it would not happen under present conditions at least. If any have tried to exercise that pressure in the past, it has never been successful. As I say, in the past the minister has had the power absolutely to refuse to renew a license at the end of the year on March 31st, and if that were done the business of that particular distiller or brewer would be wiped out. But that has never been done. In addition to that, I think most men even in public life have some sense of fairness and justice, and would not deliberately wipe out a heavy investment even of a distiller or brewer without very good reasons. We have power now to withhold the license, and it is only consistent with that power that we should have power also to cancel or suspend the license. I might explain that it was merely a coincidence that at the time of the withholding of a license of a certain brewery in the city of Toronto the books of which were not produced, its license had expired, and we did not renew it until they had paid their taxes; they did not produce their books. But if the order for the production of those books had been made a few days later, the license would have been issued in the ordinary course on the first of April, and we would not have had the
Excise Act Amendment

power to cancel or suspend it. If it was right that the minister should have the power to withhold the license at the expiration of the year, I think it is right that he should have the power to suspend or even cancel the license in case the holder abuses his privileges or his rights. I hope the leader of the opposition will not press that point too strongly. I have no particular objection to the insertion of his amendment, but frankly I do not believe it is necessary.

I am going to speak very frankly to my hon. friend. It is true that the licenses have not been cancelled, it is true that the discretion has been exercised favour ably; but it will be recalled that during the course of the investigation the auditors reported contributions to political parties by these same gentlemen. Now, just put the two things together. That is my point.
But it never resulted in the withholding of licenses.
Quite so; it resulted in something else. That is the point exactly.
My hon. friend said he was going to be frank; I wish he would be a little more frank.

The evidence before the committee did not give the details. It was pressed in certain quarters as to what were the amounts, and what they were paid for. It will be recalled that the royal commission also made certain investigations. Now, the public observing this power, and observing that licenses are always renewed, regardless of the antecedent conduct, connect the two things. That is the position. This is to make it clear that in future, misconduct followed by conviction will involve the loss of the license.
Would the hon. member say that loss would automatically follow after conviction?
No, because there might be a technical breach of the law. My hon. friend referred to such a case. I simply suggest this as being worthy of careful consideration.
I might draw to the attention of the committee that this is based directly upon the royal commission's recommendation. They did not add any proviso that there should first be a conviction.

I know that; I was looking at the recommendations to-day. Commission or no commission, the fact is that we had those things brought to our attention, and

they caused a great furore throughout the Dominion. Now every step you take that enables the public to look upon business transactions as being above suspicion is in the interest both of the public and of good government. The removal of that power under those circumstances would be something very much to be desired.

As I said before, I am not greatly prejudiced against the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman, but I do think it might occasionally delay and tie the hands of the department if it were absolutely necessary first to secure a conviction in the courts. Or this might happen: a distiller or brewer might violate the law and leave the country. You could not proceed against him, you could not cancel his license, his business would still go on, and yet it might be highly desirable that his license should be suspended. Again I wish to urge upon the committee, with due regard to what my hon. friend says, that, in a practical way, I do not believe there is any very great danger of working injustice to any brewer or distiller if this is allowed to go through as it stands.

The minister admits there
must be misconduct. Then how is the misconduct to be established? Surely the man charged should be given an opportunity of defending himself in the courts either by way of prosecution or appeal. No doubt it is a tremendous power; "the minister may for any reason he deems sufficient;" it does not even say there must be misconduct.

I suggest that the clause be allowed to stand to give the minister an opportunity to consider it further. Certainly in view of what transpired in the committee regarding the action not only of the minister but of other members of the government of the day, and of members of parliament being placed in a difficult position by their constituents-all these matters were before the committee-this is an undesirable power. It is the power of punishment without conviction; it is the exercise of the functions of a court without trial, and it affords an opportunity for pressure to be brought to bear of a kind certainly not in the public interest in connection with these matters.

I appreciate what my hon.
friend has said; but after all the committee should realize this also, that never yet has anything which he fears and dreads taken place.
I think it has.
Excise Act Amendment

Never. I am taking the
word of the commissioner of excise.

But he does not know
what we are talking about. The most flagrant violations of the act on the part of some distillers were proven before that committee. But was the licence ever suspended or cancelled? Never. "What did the evidence show? Journeys to Ottawa; representations; the licence renewed.

But I understand my hon.
friend to say that he does not desire to make it mandatory upon the minister to cancel the licence if there is a violation of the act proven in the courts. I must confess that I cannot appreciate the point which my hon. friend is trying to make.

I think my hon. friend
appreciates it all right.

A distiller may violate the
act half a dozen times and be convicted in the courts, but even then, as I understand his suggestion, the minister may not cancel or suspend the licence; the distiller can still continue his nefarious practice.

But no minister would
hesitate to cancel the licence under those circumstances. That is the point exactly.
I am not so sure.

My hon. friend would
not anyway.

No matter what has taken
place in the past, whether in the shape of political contributions or anything else-and I have not anything to say about that phase because I know nothing with regard to it-
Continue in your innocence !
-in no instance-and I am taking the word of the Commissioner of Excise-has the licence ever been withheld, no matter what party was in power.
That is my whole point.

Suppose the suggestion of
my hon. friend is adopted, if I chose, my political friends could come to me, having been convicted of violating the law once, twice or three or four times; their licences ought to be cancelled; but I do not cancel them, I still have power to decline to do so. If the hon. gentleman suggested that once a conviction has been registered against a distiller, the minister must cancel the licence, then I think there would be some teeth in the suggestion.

It is never usual to do
that in this form of statute. But this is also true, that where you have a provision with respect to a conviction, no minister dare to disregard enlightened public opinion by continuing a licence under those circumstances. It is merely the effect of public opinion upon a condition that is then known. The evidence before the committee abundantly established it. The law was set at naught, laughed at. What about the licence? The licence was all right. If there was a conviction, the effect of public opinion is all powerful with respect to the minister. We had a striking illustration of that recently in some discussions on questions of privilege that took place in this house.

It would be a dangerous
rule that upon one conviction, of any character, the license should be cancelled. A man might be convicted of a very minor offence, or the conviction might be altogether unwarranted. I have in mind the case of a brewer convicted by a magistrate whose judgment was, in my opinion, unsound. He was convicted because of some act on the part of his agent, although I do not think he was personally responsible. I submit this suggestion to the minister.

A conviction might easily
be registered once or twice, or four or five or six times, as has been the case. A good many brewers in this and other provinces have violated the provincial liquor laws as many as six times, and I venture to say-I am not referring to the government of any particular party-that there would not be very grave doubt what public opinion might be as to whether these licenses should be cancelled. I would observe this further: I believe that there is a sense of justice in most public men-I believe it characterizes those in responsible positions in charge of departments, whether they belong to one party or the other-which would restrain them from doing such a thing as my hon. friend suggests. My hon. friend has spoken about public opinion. W7ould a minister, for political reasons or for no adequate reason at all, dare to cancel a license, even if he did not have that sense of justice to which I have alluded? I cannot agree with my hon. friend that a power like this would be abused. After all, I have a good deal of faith in the sense of justice of most men; and there is the further fact that such power has never been abused in the past.

In the Customs Act you have very much the same thing. Any man who offends under that act is given an opportunity of being heard by the minister and there is
Excise Act Amendment

an appeal from the minister to the Exchequer court. But there is nothing here that indicates that the offender is to have a hearing. I do not say that the present minister would not give him a hearing; but we are discussing the act as it stands, and under that act the minister is not obliged to give him a hearing or to assign any reason. He can act upon any reason, good, bad or indifferent. There should be something in the act affording the offender an opportunity of being heard. If the minister does not like the thought of prosecution and wants to assume jurisdiction himself, let there be some provision to ensure that the offender shall be heard, just as a man is heard under the provisions of the Customs Act. Under that act he is not only heard by the minister, who gives a decision, but there is an appeal from the minister. Why not have such a provision in this act?
What does the minister think the words "public interest" mean in this connection? Would the paying of campaign funds to either of the parties be one of the offences?

I am not sure that my hon.
friend expects an answer to that.
Why not?

I am free to say I do not
think I know so much about campaign funds as my hon. friend appears to do. Certainly it would have no weight with me at all. But "in the public interest" would mean in the interest of the revenue, and I think the Department of National Revenue, when it found any brewer or distiller defrauding the revenue, should have the power to suspend the license immediately without waiting to go to the courts. I repeat, I do not think that any minister, I care not to what party he might belong, would exercise the power unjustly.
You must have proof that he is defrauding.
Public opinion would drive him from office if he committed so palpable an injustice.
But you must have proof.
And no minister would refuse a hearing.
But do you not think the act should give that right?
It would be tying the hands of the minister unduly.
You might as well say the same of the Customs Act.
What was the amount in dispute in the case referred to to-night where the license was cancelled?

Were the arrears in that case the accumulation of several years or of one year?
Two or three years.

Yes.

Hon. C. A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 194, to amend the Canadian National Railway Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Application of Railway Act to Canadian Government Railways.
Will the minister explain the scope of this proposed legislation?

Under the old section,
which will be seen in the explanatory note, the Canadian Government Railways were under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners with respect to their operation but not with respect to construction and maintenance. The object of the amendment is to put the Canadian Government Railways under the Board of Railway Commissioners as all other railways are under their control, especially with regard to the construction and maintenance of the lines. It is thought that there is now no reason for what might be called special privilege for the government railways, and when I speak of government railways I am distinguishing between them and the Canadian National Railways generally. It is understood that the Canadian National Railways generally are already under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. This section deals with the old Canadian Government Railways, the Intercolonial Railway and the National Transcontinental Railway, and seeks to bring them more completely *under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners than is now the case.
What necessity has arisen to demand this legislation?

The necessity arises
through the demands of people along the lines affected for improvements of one kind or another for which, in any other part of the country, they would secure an order from the Board of Railway Commissioners. With respect to these particular lines they find it necessary to come to the minister exactly as they did when the minister had direct control over the Intercolonial Railway and the National Transcontinental Railway.
Surely this does not apply to the Intercolonial Railway?
Yes.
Do I understand that the minister wants to be protected from the people of the maritime provinces?

No, I have no desire to be protected from the people of any part of Canada, but I do desire to give the people



C.N.R. Act Amendment
of every part of this country the same right to appear before the Board of Railway Commissioners and appeal for anything they think should be done which comes within the scope of the Railway Act. Really this simply creates a standard practice on our Canadian railways, and I think the house will agree that it is desirable that all our system should be operated in a standard manner.

We in the maritime provinces regard the Intercolonial Railway as something quite different from the other railways of this country. It is part of an agreement which was made at confederation, and there is a feeling abroad to some extent at least that we have certain obligations toward the Canadian National Railways, or in other words that we are not entitled to the benefits of competition. I should like the house and the minister to understand that the Intercolonial Railway was built for the people of the maritime provinces; it was one of the conditions of confederation, that the railway be built to serve us.

Perhaps if I were to say to my hon. friend that this amendment is not desired by the Canadian National Railways, who believe themselves to be subject to much less expense under the present system than they will be if under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, he will not regard it as something which is not in the interests of the people of the maritime provinces. The Canadian National Railways do not desire this amendment.

If they do not want it and it is going to cost more money, why have
it?

We are doing this in the interests of a standard practice, and I will point out an instance to my hon. friend. In connection with the matter of fencing, he well knows through his connection with railways what a problem this has been throughout the country. The Board of Railway Commissioners have gradually developed a standard practice in regard to ordering the railway companies to provide fences. AH down through the maritime provinces that problem still exists, and under this amendment the Board of Railway Commissioners will have power to order the company to build the fences. I submit that there is no reason why the people of that part of Canada should not have the same right to apply to the Board of Railway Commissioners for an order against the railway company, just as the people in any other part of Canada do. It is also desirable that the same regulations with re-

gard to clearances, for example, should be operative on all the railways of Canada. It is unfortunate, perhaps, but in some of the communities served by the Intercolonial Railway, due largely to the period in our history when the railway was built, the clearances are not as complete and free as they have become since on the railways generally under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I think everyone will agree that it is desirable to have standard clearances throughout Canada, and under this amendment the Board of Railway Commissioners will have power to see that the clearances along the Intercolonial railway are standardized. The National Transcontinental, of course, was built at a later period and consequently has greater clearances. I give these merely as instances. My friend the leader of the opposition is correct in saying it may cost the Canadian National more money to comply with orders which the Board of Railway Commissioners may make; but inasmuch as similar orders are already being made throughout Canada, I see no reason why the people of the maritime provinces should not have the protection of the same orders and standard devices which prevail elsewhere throughout Canada.
I understand that standard orders as to clearances and so on are in force already throughout Canada.
That is not quite correct.

I have not recently been over the road as frequently as I used to be, but from 1912 on the clearances were standard, and everything else was done under the same rules and regulations as though it were under the Board of Railway Commissioners. At one time I advocated in the house the bringing of the Intercolonial under the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I believed it was right. Subsequently I changed my mind, because I realized that the Intercolonial was different from any other railway in Canada; that it owed its being to the provisions of the pact by which its construction was provided for. I cannot understand what i3 behind this. If it is going to cost more money and nobody is asking for it, why should we do it?

My hon. friend is correct except in this respect: as applying to construction and maintenance, these railways are not and never have been under the Board of Railway Commissioners. Difficulties arise every few months, I may say, particularly in respect to labour unions, on matters of maintenance. That is another point which I did not mention before. Standard methods and practice are of importance to labour and labour

C.N.R. Act Amendment
unions. At present the government railways are under the Board of Railway Commissioners with respect to management and operation. and with respect to maintenance so far as the safety and protection of railway employees and passengers upon the railway are affected; but always there are questions of interpretation, as to whether or not the particular matter of maintenance under discussion is one which affects the safety of passengers and employees. By this amendment we eliminate that question of interpretation altogether and make the Board of Railway Commissioners the judges of what is needed.
In other words you substitute some other engineer for the railway's engineer.
If my hon. friend is right, we might as well eliminate all the expenses of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

As a matter of fact, they do very little. The Canadian Pacific Railway maintains a higher standard than is required; then there is the rock ballast of the National railway line also to Chicago. What I cannot understand is why this should be done, having in mind what the minister has said.

I thought it was so selfapparent that it would require no explanation. If other members of the committee share my hon. friend's view, and if there is no demand for a standard of maintenance, I should like to know of it. I thought this was something so much in the public interest that I was taking a forward step in bringing about the same conditions in the maritime provinces as exist elsewhere in this regard. If it is desired to let railways decide their own standards of maintenance and construction, let parliament say so.

I do not say that; the
hon. genlleman cannot get away with that sort of thing. When he talks about the standard of maintenance he knows very well he is talking piffle. The standard of maintenance between Toronto and Montreal is different altogether from that which prevails in other parts of Canada, and the standard is one which the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific do not respect, because their standard is much better. In this country, under any system of government, the Canadian National Railway is bound to provide for the Intercolonial such a standard of efficiency as the traffic demands. I admit I am taking up too much time in talking about it, but what I am anxious to know is who is wanting it. The minister says the railway does not want it.

I must object to my hon. friend's word when he says I am talking "piffle" in advocating the standardization of practice and equipment. There is a minimum standard set up, as he well knows, by the railway commission. Will he argue for a moment that the setting up of that minimum of standard by the Board of Railway Commissioners has not tended throughout the years to improve the general standard of construction and maintenance throughout Canada? Of course he will not.

I would say at once, no, it has not. The standard which now prevails on both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific is higher than that laid down by the Board of Railway Commissioners, as to rail, fastenings, roadbed, class and kind of ballast, and structures and approaches.
But not on the Intercolonial in all cases.
I will tell you where you will find the minimum-on some branch lines in western Canada.

On some of the branch
lines on the Intercolonial. If the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) were here to-night, he would tell my hon. friend all the refusals, from his point of view, for instance,-and there are others,-of the Canadian National to do wliat the Board of Railway Commissioners would order them to do were they under the jurisdiction of the board, in the matter of fences, for instance. I have mentioned the representation of the unions with regard to the matter of standards of maintenance on the Intercolonial lines. I believe I am correct in saying that that particular matter has been adjusted, for the reason that I took it up with the railway; but I cannot see any reason why, with respect to this particular part of the Canadian National system, the management should be able to say: We do not have to take any notice of the Board of Railway Commissioners, whereas with respect to the rest of the same system they are compelled to do so. I should like to hear an expression of opinion from the rest of the committee, because if this is not a proper step to take, I should like to know it.

We have a general opinion in the maritime provinces that we have suffered in recent years because the road has been taken over and operated as it has, and naturally or unnaturally we are a little suspicious of any additional changes which will further put the railway under the control
199S
C.N.R. Act Amendment

of any other department, whether it be the Board of Railway Commissioners or any other. We would prefer to have the Intercolonial railway as we had it before unholy hands were laid on it ten or fifteen years ago, or say before 1912. The explanation, so far as I can see, appears all right. I do not know that the proposed change is going to interfere very much, but I am not sure that I see all the way through it, and I would prefer to leave the situation as it was.
Will the minister explain the reference to the Expropriation Act in the last few lines of the bill?

The difference between the expropriation procedure under the Railway Act and under the Government Railways Act I think I can put briefly in this way-and some of the legal members may help me out if I get off the track a little in my terminology. If the government railways undertake to expropriate property they may surrender that property again to the former owner and are liable only for any damages which may have accrued during the period of occupancy of the government railways. If expropriation proceedings are taken under the terms of the general Railway Act, the expropriation once made confirms the ownership of the property in the railway. They must pay for the property and then of course they have the right to sell it, but they cannot hand it back in the same manner as the crown can do under the ordinary crown expropriation procedure which applies to the Canadian Government Railways Act.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

Hon. W D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 198, to amend the Customs Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon. Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Vessels found hovering in territorial waters may be boarded and brought into port.

Subclause (2) reads:
Any vessel in territorial waters of Canada, shall bring to when required so to do in the king's name.
Is "bring to" the proper term?

I am told so.
.'Mr. Oantley.]
I have always heard that "heave to" is the proper term. It is the term used in admiralty cases.
The matter was discussed in the office the other day and I was assured by the chief official there that "bring to" was the proper term.

In the English statutes, in the English cases and under the admiralty jurisdiction the term used is that the ship is ordered to "heave to". I have never seen the term "bring to". It may be technically correct.

I do not think there is any
doubt as to the meaning.

According to the clause I do not think "bring to" means anything. The subclause reads:
Any vessel in territorial waters of Canada, shall bring to when required so to do in the king's name by any officer or upon signal made by any government vessel or cruiser by hoisting the pennant and ensign approved and appointed for the purpose by order of the governor in council.
Of course, what it is intended to do is clear. The vessel, if it is a sailing vessel, must come up in the wind and thereby lose headway. If it is a steamer, this means that she must stop. I think it is desirable to use some term that will give rise to no uncertainty.
If it were a steamer, "heave to" would not be as appropriate as "bring to."

No, the word "stop" is
right.
"Heave to" is the proper term.

The matter was discussed
in the department and the officials there seemed to know a good deal about it. I am quite willing to accept the opinion of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough.

If the hon. member for
Antigonish-Guysborough will follow me, I think the term "heave to" is proper with respect to sailing ships.
Quite right.

But with respect to a
steamer I think the idea should be made perfectly clear. Motor boats or vessels using secondary power are supposed on demand to shut off their steam or other motive power and come to a standstill.

Why not use a plain English
word and say "stop?"

Customs Act Amendment

That is exactly what I
was going to say. In the case of a steamer it should stop; in the case of a sailing vessel it should heave to.

You want the vessel to stop
in either case. Why not use the word "stop" in both cases.

You cannot stop a vessel
which has sails.
Why not say "heave to, bring to, or stop?"

I think the clause is all
right the way it is.
Will the minister explain what is meant by territorial waters?

I made that explanation as
well as I could on Tuesday. It is explained
on page 2 of the bill. Subclause (7) reads:
Tei i itorial waters of Canada shall mean the waters forming part of the territory of the Dominion of Canada and the waters adjacent to the Dominion within three miles thereof.

I appealed to the minister before in regard to this whole question. So long as the customs and excise duties are as high as they are to-day you cannot stop smuggling in the maritime provinces. For instance, Nova Scotia has two thousand miles of coast line. If the minister had a hundred protective vessels and a thousand coastguards on the coast of the maritime provinces he could not stop the smuggling of liquor. But the Minister of Customs can stop it overnight by reducing the duty to what it was ten years ago, S2.40. If he will turn up the speech that the Hon. Mr. Fielding made the last time he changed the duty, he will find there a wealth of information based on experience. While I am not able to quote verbatim what Mr. Fielding said at the time, in effect, it was this: He increased the duty from $1.80 to $2.40, and he said that he was convinced that he had put the duty as high as, and he rather thought higher than, was in the country's interest, and he was absolutely sure that he had reached the limit. He had had some considerable experience. He knew the conditions, and continuing he said he might be asked why, if he viewed the matter that way, why he was raising the duty, and he said that he was making the change at the solicitation of his temperance friends who thought that an increased duty would be conducive towards greater sobriety in the country. I submit that it has not had that effect, that on the contrary it has had the opposite effect, and I tell the minister, in all seriousness, that he will never be able to stop this smuggling with the duty
remaining as high as it is to-day, because human nature is the same everywhere, whether it be in the maritime provinces or on the great lakes. While $10 a gallon is imposed on spirits coming into this country and while the customs duty on a case of whiskey costing say S14 is 821 or more, which in the case of West India rum means a duty of 1,000 per cent of the value, smuggling cannot be stopped. You can buy rum at Demerara of first class' quality for one dollar a gallon or less. That is the situation to-day, and the minister might as well face it. I understood from the minister last year and the year before that the duty would be reduced simply for the reasons I am outlining now, and I would like to know why it has not been done.
Does the hon. gentleman say that I made the statement in thp house that the duty would be reduced?
The minister in charge at the time.
I was in charge last year.
Well then, I think the conversation was with you.

Subsection 7 of section 1 says:
(7) For the purposes of this section and section two hundred and seven of this act, ''territorial waters of Canada", shall mean the waters forming part of the territory of the Dominion of Canada and the waters adjacent to the Dominion within three marine miles thereof, in the case of any vessel, and within twelve marine miles thereof, in the case of any vessel registered in Canada.
Does this mean we are going to have two rum rows, one three miles out and the other twelve miles out? If so, how on earth are you going to enforce the law? What is the advantage of that subsection?

As the law now stands, vessels registered in Canada can hover around the three mile limit awaiting an opportunity to discharge their cargoes into smaller boats. If we can make them stay twelve miles out from our coast, we have a little better opportunity of watching them and seizing their cargoes.
Would not this result in more Canadian vessels coming under foreign registry?
I do not think so.

I doubt if subsection 7 will
have any real effect. I am still of the opinion I expressed the other day, that the jurisdiction of Canada, even over its own nationals, is
Customs Act Amendment

territorial. It is an accepted fact that only sovereign states have jurisdiction over their own nationals extraterritorially, and ships would come within the same category once they get beyond the borders of the country. I am firmly of the opinion that that portion of the act which permits the seizure of a vessel of Canadian registry outside the three mile limit, as it is called, will be held ultra vires by the courts. I do not think that even since the last imperial conference we can be classed as a sovereign country. Certainly there is nothing which would induce the courts to change the opinion they have formed, and they have definitely held that the jurisdiction of non-sovereign states is purely territorial. Great Britain has jurisdiction over its own nationals, or at least can punish them for offences committed outside of Great Britain on the high seas, but once our ships leave the three mile limit they come under British mercantile law. My opinion is that subsection 7 is not going to accomplish anything, but if it does, all it will do will be to make ships of Canadian registry register in the United States or at St. Pierre. If the_minister were at all conversant with the conditions he would surely realize from the outset that the clause is futile.

I spoke on this the other
night. As I said, I am not a constitutional lawyer or any other kind of lawyer, and I am not in a position to express any legal opinion. But I should think it at least regrettable if the Dominion government has not control over its own vessels.
It is time it had, but it has not.
The Minister of Justice will probably like to make some comments upon this, and I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Perhaps he would look
into the expression "bring to" at the same time.
Progress reported.
